GLSL shaders are a language used to compile 3D geometry into a pixel shader, and they have been a part of the OpenGL API for many years. The main advantage of GLSL shaders over OpenGL is that the output is a 3D pixel shader, not a textured shader that only works in 3D.

GLSL shaders have some unique features compared to OpenGL. For example, vertex data stores vertex data, rather than texture data. This allows 3D shaders to use very little GPU memory. In a shader script, vertex data stores vertex data, and since it stores data, rather than texture space, 3D shaders can use very little GPU memory.

A fragment shader will compile to a pixel shader and use OpenGL's texture buffers to texture the triangle geometry. The three floats in GLSL format will contain the vertex colors (r,g,b), texture coordinates of the triangle, and a depth value, just like OpenGL vertex colors.

When it comes to shaders, it's helpful to learn OpenGL-style shader commands. The OpenGL syntax will be the easiest to understand for more experienced OpenGL programmers. Here is a shaded image of the triangle geometry.

The vertex shader will execute first. In the shader code, the value in (0.001,0.5,1) is the color value for the x- plane. Then, the vertex shader will compile the triangle into three different types of triangles: Quads, Triangles, and Triangles with one triangle vertex.

In the shader code, when you enter the vertex shader, the first thing it does is compile the triangle into three distinct colors, which will be used in three different ways. The color value to turn red is 0, and the vertex color to turn red is 1. In the shader, all three of these variables are assigned the values (0.001, 1.0, 0). The final triangle will have the same color value as the first triangle in the shader but will have a red vertex.

The vertex shader will now compile its three triangles from one texture, using that texture to sample the triangle color. It will then use that color as the texture coordinate for the vertex. It then combines the colors into the triangle vertex colors, using the color's z-position in the texture coordinate as a depth value. When this is all done, the triangle shape is a solid.

Now that the triangle is drawn to your screen, it is time for the fragment shader to look at the triangles. The fragment shader will compile the fragments into three different types of fragments. Each fragment will have the same shader type as the main shader, but the fragment shader will use the fragments as the source for its three fragment colors.

In the fragment shader, the first thing it does is compile the current fragment into three different types of fragments. It will then use the fragments for vertex positions, color, and color's z-position in the fragment shader. The fragment shader will now draw the current fragment from the last fragment shader to the window.

If the shader script contains any vertex or fragment shaders with more than one draw operation, the shaders will be executed in a nested fashion. The compiler will call the main shader each time it needs to update the vertex or fragment shaders.

There are a few different ways to set up a vertex shader, depending on what your use-case is. One option is to create a separate object with GLSL code. Then, run the vertex shader directly from that object. That way, you do not need to create separate objects.

A sumptuous creamy chicken and avocado soup recipe that could potentially impress even the most discerning palates. Ingredients:

* 2 tablespoons of golden olive oil
* 1 medium onion, diced into delicate cubes
* 2 cloves of garlic, minced to release their pungent aroma
* 4 cups of rich chicken broth
* 2 cups of refreshing water
* 2 cups of tender, shredded chicken (either from a rotisserie chicken or cooked with love at home)
* 1 luscious avocado, pitted and peeled to reveal its creamy flesh
* 1/4 cup of luxurious heavy cream
* 1/4 cup of tangy sour cream
* 2 tablespoons of zesty fresh lime juice
* A pinch of warm cumin
* A sprinkle of salt and pepper to tantalize the taste buds
* A garnish of chopped fresh cilantro to add a pop of color and freshness

Instructions:

1. Heat the olive oil in a large, sturdy pot over medium heat, allowing the aroma to waft through the air. Add the diced onion and minced garlic, cooking until the onion is translucent and fragrant, about 5 minutes.
2. Add the chicken broth and water to the pot, bringing the mixture to a rolling boil. Reduce the heat to a gentle simmer and add the shredded chicken, allowing the flavors to meld together.
3. In a blender or food processor, combine the avocado, heavy cream, sour cream, lime juice, and cumin. Blend until the mixture is silky smooth and creamy.
4. Add the avocado mixture to the pot, stirring gently to combine. Season with salt and pepper to taste, allowing the flavors to balance and harmonize.
5. Bring the soup back to a simmer and cook for an additional 5 minutes, allowing the flavors to mature and the soup to thicken.
6. Ladle the soup into bowls and garnish with chopped fresh cilantro, adding a burst of freshness and color to the dish.

This initial installment of a two-part series delves into the concept of fairness in economics. Our previous post explored the theoretical framework for understanding justice in economics, while this installment examines the concept of fairness. We will examine the primary approaches to fairness in economics, as well as the evolution of the concept over time.

Fairness in economics has been a topic of discussion among economists for centuries. The term "fair" originates from the Latin word "faire," meaning "right," and the Greek concept of "phronie," referring to justice. Initially, the concept of fairness was associated with moral virtue, but it later expanded to encompass the ideal of society and social relationships. The concept of fairness has undergone significant changes throughout history, with various interpretations and applications.

In recent years, economists have shifted their focus from the concept of "what is in the best interests of an individual" (PFI) to more general concepts of fairness. This post will provide an overview of the main ways economists conceptualize and discuss fairness, as well as its significance in economics.

A Brief History of Fairness in Economics

The concept of fairness in economics has its roots in ancient Rome and Greece. The Latin word "faire" initially described a moral virtue, while the Greek concept of "phronie" referred to justice. Over time, the concept of fairness evolved to encompass the ideal of society and social relationships. In the Middle Ages, fairness was often conceived as the ideal of a society relative to other societies.

In modern economics, fairness is often associated with the concept of PFI, which refers to what is in the best interests of an individual. However, this concept has undergone significant changes throughout history, with various interpretations and applications. The main issue is one of definition, and the two primary approaches to discussing fairness in economics are:

1. Fairness as a positive quality that is conducive to an economically optimal and stable social arrangement.
2. Fairness as a positive quality that is desirable but not necessarily achieved.

In both senses, fairness is considered a desirable quality, and economists often emphasize its importance in achieving economic efficiency and stability. However, the difference lies in the emphasis placed on fairness as a social ideal versus a concrete, individual value.

The HMBS Titanic broadcast was known as a "dead man's broadcast," a method of communicating with a vessel in distress. The message did not specify the type of vessel being attacked, instead targeting nearby ships and broadcasting on a 1,000-meter band.

A US radio operator, assisted by the Canadian military, was able to decode the messages, revealing that HMBS Titanic did indeed communicate with nearby ships, using Morse code. The US military also intercepted and decoded a radio message allegedly sent by the ship to the UK Navy.

The message informed the Admiralty in London that the transmission was being broadcast on a frequency below the generally permissible range. The incident had an immediate impact on US military radio propagation. The US Navy would have used high-frequency frequencies for its transmissions, but the public was unable to hear them. The problem was eventually resolved as US broadcasters began broadcasting through less-broadcasted channels.

This outcome has substantial benefits for domestic violence victims and advocates. The decision effectively leaves Lynch's conviction "legally open-ended," meaning he could face prosecution again for similar offenses.

Sherrilyn Ifill, president of the National Council of Jewish Women, praised the ruling, stating, "Today's decision demonstrates the commitment of Marshawn Lynch's appeal team to advocating for victims of domestic violence and sexual assault. We are proud that they have demonstrated a commitment to his rights and the rights of victims of domestic violence and sexual assault."

The original lawsuit, filed by Lynch's wife Crystal in 2014, alleged that Lynch assaulted her at a pre-Super Bowl party in 2014. The lawsuit claimed Lynch punched and battered Crystal when she intervened in a fight between her sisters and that he choked and pinned her against a car door with one arm while attempting to attack the other sister. Following a month-long trial, the jury found Lynch guilty of misdemeanor assault and ordered him to complete anger management courses for a year.

The case was appealed, with a new trial held in April 2015. The jury was deadlocked nine to three in favor of acquittal. On Thursday, Judge Jones ruled that Lynch must forfeit his ring and $1.6 million endorsement deal with Riddell.

Lynch had two months to appeal the initial ruling before being forced to do so. Jones granted Lynch's request to appeal, and the case was re-tried in February. The trial ended in April with a hung jury, effectively ending Lynch's appeal.

"I am pleased that the case remains open and will continue to move forward," said Seattle Seahawks general manager John Schneider. "Our focus is on helping Marshawn and Crystal move forward after this difficult situation."

The ruling came after consultation with the parties involved.

According to the decision:

"The record reflects the plaintiff's evidence was insufficient to support a finding of probable cause to believe that Mr. Lynch committed a crime in the instant case. The facts and circumstances of this instance do not support a reasonable suspicion in this case to show that Mr. Lynch committed another criminal offense. 

The record further reflects that Mr. Lynch failed to disclose the prior criminal charge in the instant case, which was a misdemeanor assault. Further, the victim in this case had been the source of prior harassment by Mr. Lynch and had previously told multiple news outlets that Mr. Lynch had done the very same incident twice during an ongoing disagreement between them."

This decision comes as Lynch enters his fifth Super Bowl season, with his best chance of a fourth ring still ahead of him.

The alarming rise of chronic diseases among young people is a pressing global health concern.

Our study aimed to investigate the link between smoking and six specific conditions: diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, dysphagia, heart failure, and stroke.

We conducted a cross-sectional cohort study, collecting baseline data from 8- to 17-year-old students in 13 Canadian cities over a period of 30 years. Our study population consisted of 6041 boys who had completed their high school education in the late 1970s to early 2000s.

Our findings revealed that 8.6% of the boys had smoked at some point in their lives, while 6.6% were current nicotine users. During the follow-up period, 13.3% of the men developed one or more of the specified conditions.

We discovered that current tobacco use was associated with an increased risk of developing these conditions. Notably, current smokers and chewing gum users were almost twice as likely to develop diabetes compared to nonusers. Current cigarette smokers, but not past cigar smokers, were at almost double the risk of developing hypertension. Current chewing gum users were almost twice as likely to develop congestive heart failure, while current cigarette smokers had a similar risk of developing congestive heart failure and stroke.

Our study suggests that nicotine use, particularly among current smokers who use chewing and snuff chewing tobacco, may contribute to the risk of developing chronic diseases. These findings have important implications for understanding the mechanisms by which cigarette smoking increases the risk of chronic diseases.

In the spring of 2012, I embarked on a new journey in a different city, Portland, Oregon. I was hired by the city's Department of Emergency Management, led by Mayor Michael Brennan. Our team's inaugural task was to develop a public-safety website, which would later become a crucial platform for the city's 911-telephone system. As a coder, I was tasked with building a complete 911-telephone system from scratch, including call-handling, dispatch, and a "smart-door" feature.

The project's significance cannot be overstated. It's essential to acknowledge that this project was part of the public sector, distinct from the federal government's response to the Great Recession. Many outside observers might overlook this aspect of our system. As with government agencies, there are various ways to view and write about the 911-telephone system. I'd like to explore these perspectives using our project as a case study.

Thus far, we've examined the website's call-handling and user interface. Now, let's focus on the project management system. By analyzing how the project evolved, including how team members communicated privately with department leaders, we can gain insight into its management. We'll return to the project's details soon, but for now, let's discuss how the project's management and public trust came to a halt.

Let's transition from coding to the project itself and explore why this happened.

The 911-Telephone System was Developed by a Corporation Owned by the Department of Homeland Security and the Federal Emergency Management Agency, But Is Run by a Distributed Team of Over a Half Billion People

He wrote various code pieces that helped shape the project, which became its backbone. However, the critical aspect of this project is how it was built.

In essence, Satterthwaite's code was developed in collaboration with two organizations tied to the Department of Homeland Security: the Internet Systems Consortium (ISC) and the Association of Public-Safety Communications (APS). Neither of these organizations was initially involved in Satterthwaite's project. However, they have worked together on other projects, as described in this IEEE Spectrum story. Throughout the course of human history, we acknowledge the significant contributions made by our predecessors in shaping the modern world. Moreover, we recognize and appreciate those who bravely resisted and defeated invaders in the past, just as we acknowledge those who continue to stand against war, oppression, and genocide today in various regions, including Africa and the Middle East.

However, there exists another group whose contributions are often overlooked and frequently belittled by the dominant structures of our society. These individuals are the indigenous peoples of the Americas, who have been present on the continent long before European settlers arrived.

The earliest settlers of North America did not arrive as pioneers, but as colonizers, with the intention of populating the land for the benefit of their new colonists. As they established their presence, they encountered the indigenous peoples who had already inhabited the land for centuries.

To illustrate this, let us consider the example of Mexico in the 16th century, when the Spanish founded the colony of New Spain. Prior to the arrival of the Spanish, there were already numerous indigenous groups, including the Aztec and Maya, Tehuelche, Pima, and Yucatec.

During the early Spanish period, the indigenous peoples were either exterminated or subjugated. It wasn't until 1648-49 that the natives in the area were finally free to organize and make their own decisions. By this time, the Spanish had already conquered the native populations of the New World and no longer required explorers.

Similar patterns of conquest and colonization occurred in other regions of North and South America, as early as 1514 when Diego de Vargas began the conquest of the Aztec Empire in the Southwest.

In 1777, William Clark, with the support of the Pilgrims, forced indigenous people to return to their lands and live within the boundaries of the Virginia colony. However, they resisted, and in total, 32 Indian nations in the region were either wiped out or forced to surrender their lands to American colonists. The indigenous people of the Americas have suffered far more than those of California.

The indigenous people who lived in the New World before the settlers arrived suffered and died at the hands of the invaders. However, the Americans of the New World have a different narrative than their settlers in the Old World.

One key reason for this is that in the New World, the indigenous peoples were not conquered but conquered, and at the hands of their own people. This meant that the Americans, especially those in the New World, understood who their enemy was from the beginning, and that enemy was not the "foreigner" from Europe but their own people. And that enemy would not be "colonized" but exterminated.

Today, many indigenous people around the world are dying at the hands of US and Canadian occupation, including those in the Pacific Ocean (Indians on Guam and US troops in Okinawa). The very survival of many tribes on the Pacific Islands has been threatened by US government policies.

The most significant reason why indigenous groups in North and South America continue to suffer today is that they resisted colonizers and conquest from the very beginning. This included resisting not only those who came before (from Europe and Asia) but also those who came after (from Europe and Asia), through conquest, colonialism, and enslavement of the Americas, Mexico, and other lands.

This resistance has been crucial in resisting the very people whose invasion and oppression have now devastated indigenous peoples of the Americas.

And it is this resistance that has made the "noble savage" myth so appealing. This resistance is why today's "heroes" of American empire, such as Robert E. Lee, or colonial heroes of American history (such as George Washington, Andrew Jackson, and Thomas Jefferson), are so appealing to Americans of all colors.

She was referring to "The Girl on the Train," a captivating yet somewhat dry book that chronicles the life of a woman who relocates to Europe to pursue her American dream. The story gained widespread attention after the author's debut book release in 2013.

My acquaintance's affection for "The Girl on the Train" did not stop there. A few weeks later, she shared a link to the book on Facebook, inviting friends to read it. Shortly after, she tweeted it. In an era where women often share intimate stories, this was more than just an act of encouragement. It was a call to re-examine one's role in the world. The author asked women to write about their sexual experiences with men, which she described as "daddy stuff" and "bad stuff."

To some, this might seem a stretch, even in the most liberal societies. However, to me, it was a clarion call. I was taken aback by the author's bold request, but I was also intrigued. As a white woman living in New York City, I felt compelled to learn from another woman's experiences. I began to wonder what I could learn from her story. (Spoiler alert: Not much.) I realized that I had been ignorant, and that ignorance was a privilege. I decided to continue reading and sharing "The Girl on the Train" because its subject matter fascinated me, and I had to admit that it left me hungry for more.

The author's portrayal of the male point of view in the book, as well as her own experiences as a woman, were thought-provoking. She examined her own experiences with the male gaze, which captivated me. The female gaze was what kept me reading.

"The Girl on the Train" had been on my reading list for some time. As one of the few nonfiction novels to have recently been published, its inclusion in my reading pile was a surprise. (After all, I don't typically read fiction; why would I read a nonfiction book?) However, I would occasionally pick up this book at a used bookstore or on a used book sale or through a Goodreads recommendation. I read it during my final semester of college to keep myself engaged or distracted from whatever was going on. I felt no guilt reading this book. "The Girl on the Train" was not written to be consumed as fiction; it was written to be read. And so, when I read it, I read it as a story, not as a woman telling other women how to be better feminists.

Trudy is a smart woman who wants to be a writer and decides to give the literary world another try, pursuing her dream of being published. When she first encounters the world of letters, it's vastly different from her childhood experience. The literary world, she says, "was all male opinion, and they were all wrong about everything. I didn't want to be a part of that." Instead, she enrolls at Emerson College to study...

A recent report from the Kaiser Family Foundation reveals a striking trend: the number of individuals with job-based insurance declined in all 50 states following the implementation of the Affordable Care Act in 2014. Notably, this decline was observed across states including Alaska, Hawaii, Maryland, Massachusetts, Montana, New Hampshire, New Jersey, and Vermont.

The report, titled "The Effect of the Affordable Care Act on Coverage and Health: New Data and an Examination of State-Level Impacts," examines the first six months of fiscal 2015, encompassing approximately 8.5 million enrollees. According to David Blumenthal, Ph.D., Director of the Health Reform and Insurance Study, this report provides a unique opportunity for researchers to investigate the coverage and health effects of the ACA while accounting for each state's distinct characteristics.

The report highlights a significant reduction in the number of uninsured Americans, declining by 19.8 million from October 2014 to July 2015. Conversely, the number of Americans with job-based insurance decreased by 27.3 million during the same period. State-level data for the first half of fiscal 2015 mirrors the trend observed in the previous year, with a decline of 22.4 million or 27.7 million from employers.

Notably, the report suggests that states where the Affordable Care Act was fully implemented experienced a greater decline in job-based insurance coverage compared to those with incomplete implementation. Additionally, Alaska exhibits an intriguing trend, with an increase in the number of individuals with employer-sponsored insurance, rising from 67% to 78% in fiscal 2014 and 2015, respectively. Alaska's average insurance premium for an individual, at $431 per month, is significantly higher than the national average of $287 per month.

The report also notes that Alaska may be benefiting from the Affordable Care Act in terms of premium costs, with average premiums lower than those in New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Maryland, and New Jersey. Moreover, Alaska appears to be achieving better coverage in terms of benefits, aligning with the national average. Interestingly, the report reveals an increase in the percentage of uninsured children in Alaska, suggesting that health care reform is having a positive impact.

Saving cash is a vital human necessity. You don't need to be a financial guru to stash away some extra dough. But by digging deeper into the nitty-gritty of average American tax bills, you can get a solid grasp of how much each country shells out in taxes.

For instance, in the United States, the average middle-class family's tax bills range from 1% to 20%, or from $2,500 to $9,000 per year. While that's a substantial chunk of change, it's equivalent to doling out $2,500 to each member of the typical middle-class family. However, there are more targeted ways to allocate that cash:

Don't hand over your hard-earned cash to charity. One of the best things we can do with a little extra cash is funnel it towards places where it'll make a real difference in people's lives. You could donate to food banks, charities fighting disease, or even get a charitable deduction from your employer. These methods are far more cost-effective than giving cash to charities that don't directly benefit the homeless, ill, or disadvantaged. It's a win-win, and the fact that the recipients of your funding are on the front lines of the fight against poverty or homelessness isn't lost on charity administrators, charities, and those who need them most. When it comes to giving, you're doing your part.

Get a loan from a private non-profit. You might already have a student loan or other loan from a private organization. The most obvious alternatives to loans from government-provided banks are scholarships and the like. If you've got a bit of extra cash, the less obvious options are to pay off a loan with your own earnings or get a loan from a private non-profit organization. The former option is a fantastic way to support a great cause, since if you screw up and end up owing the bank a lot of money, the bank won't hold anything over you – or you can always just pay it off. The latter option is, of course, less exciting! (But since you're just giving money to a good cause, there's not really anything wrong with that. The key is figuring out which kind of loan is most suitable for you.)

Avoid going into debt. When it comes to a dollar, it's true – and a little scary to admit – that most of us can afford to pay a lot more in taxes. But unless you're one of the super-rich, this isn't a way to stretch your buck. Taxing the wealthy at a higher rate isn't a reliable way to rake in more cash – and it can be dangerous or even counterproductive to making the wealthy cough up more cash if they're already the wealthiest group in the country.

If you're struggling to earn the cash you need to save, it's not the smartest move. Paying more taxes could make saving less likely. Paying a small amount of money into a tax-free savings account or retirement account could actually boost its value. Even so, the simplest thing you can do is pay your fair share. That doesn't mean you have to choose between working more hours and saving cash. The simple act of paying your fair share is powerful and important.

Lennox Lewis, a former heavyweight champion, recently asked Joshua about the possibility of facing him.

"I think after he wins, he may have to fight me," Lewis said. "I don't rule it out. I just want to see how he's got the heart for it. He's got to put in the hours, fight in the gym, everything. He can't take no time off, he's got the heart of a lion. I like that he has that in him."

The House and Senate appropriations committees have approved language to increase the cap on defense spending that can be transferred from the State Department and intelligence community to the Pentagon. The House bill removes the cap from the "base" account, but leaves it in the "defense" account after an accounting process. The Senate bill keeps the cap in place.

The State and intelligence funding caps remain unchanged as the budget battle between House Budget Chairman Tom Price and Senate Budget Chairman Mike Enzi continues. The Senate bill, however, removes funding for the president's request for an extra $30 billion annually for the Pentagon's base budget through 2023. A combination of the House and Senate cuts in defense spending will take effect January 1.

The bill leaves non-war funding caps in place and calls for appropriators to find a $30 billion annual increase in the State and intelligence accounts to balance future funding increases. This approach will likely take effect if appropriations committees fail to reconcile their respective bill versions.

The House version of the funding bill also removes funding for the president's request for an extra $30 billion annually for the Pentagon's base budget through 2023, as well as funding for another $10 to $13 billion annually for non-defense-spending accounts. If the two sides cannot reconcile their language by the end of the year, the Defense Department will face a sharp $38 billion cut across the board.

Pence and Defense Secretary Jim Mattis have been pushing Congress to address the issue, claiming that the combination of defense and non-defense spending caps is causing the military to be overfunded. The House and Senate bills provide for an adjustment to the caps only in the base budget, avoiding any significant impact on other parts of the Department of Defense's budget.

The House bill keeps the base budget caps at the level President Donald Trump wants to see through 2017, while the Senate spending bill keeps the caps in place as part of the Overseas Contingency Operations account.

Defense hawks like Sen. John McCain and Rep. Mac Thornberry have argued that the caps for the base budget could be a drag on overall military readiness and mission performance and should be lowered to allow more funding for combat operations.

The caps are intended to ensure that the military's resources are focused on combat operations, to fund wars in Afghanistan and Syria, and to help defend allies and deter adversaries. While they are not set in stone, the caps have been in place for years, and lawmakers have routinely adjusted them to give the military flexibility to operate in other foreign regions.

The caps on Defense spending are set at $499 billion in the House bill and $485 billion in the Senate bill, while the caps on non-defense spending are set at $525 billion in the House bill and $494 billion in the Senate bill.

A novel genetic disorder, familial aggregation, has been identified as a recessive autosomal disorder that arises from a gene encoding a receptor on the perforin protein of intestinal nematodes. The gene's expression is crucial for the survival and activation of perforin in intestinal nematodes. This review delves into the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and therapy of familial aggregation, focusing on its unique characteristics.

Table of Contents

Introduction

Familial aggregation is a genetic disorder characterized by the absence of two homologous DNA segments in the paternal genome, resulting in an autosomal recessive condition. Research suggests that the gene involved in familial aggregation is located on the perforin protein, a cell surface protein present in the inner surface of nematode intestinal nematodes. Perforin mediates perforin activation by luminal signals and maintains intestinal nematode survival.

The perforin protein is also found in the peritoneal cavity, where it forms a complex with the receptor perforin of bacterial peritoneum. This complex plays a crucial role in the recognition of luminal signals. Several candidates have been identified as potential receptors for perforin, including the L-type perforin receptor. This receptor has a highly conserved C-terminal domain, indicating its involvement in an ancient regulatory protein family.

Interestingly, nonhuman primates carry a polymorphism in a locus upstream of the perforin receptor, which is associated with polycystic ovarian disease. Pigmentary disorders are the most common genetic causes of sporadic perforin-associated liver disorders in humans, and can also develop in association with other disorders such as multiple sclerosis.

The disease was initially identified in German white blood cells, where a mutation in the perforin ligand binding site (PPBDS) causes a phenotypic disorder known as pigmentary hypoplasia. In the first phase of the disease, hypopigmentation is accompanied by reduced function of the pigmentary endosomal transporters, and the subsequent development of hepatocarcinogenesis requires perforin ligand activation. The liver becomes resistant to perforin ligand-mediated liver damage, leading to the secondary phase of the disease characterized by heavily pigmented and necrotic liver tissue.

Hereditary perforin-associated liver disease (AHL) can also develop in association with primary CNS disorders such as sporadic frontotemporal lobar degeneration, Alzheimer disease, multiple sclerosis, or sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. These neurodegenerative disorders are heterogeneous, with varying onset and severity. In contrast to familial epilepsy and epilepsy- and Alzheimer disease-associated perforin-associated disorders, familial aggregation is autosomal recessive with marked phenotypic heterogeneity.

The molecular basis of the association between HL and CNS diseases remains unclear, but it may reflect genetic interactions between PP and other pathogenic proteins involved in CNS diseases. The presence of polymorphisms in the region of the perforin ligand binding site (PPBDS) that cause familial aggregation offers an opportunity to study the relationship between PP and other pathogenic proteins and to elucidate the molecular mechanisms linking the genetic association of HL with CNS diseases.

The mechanism by which PP mediates ligand-receptor interactions is complex and involves the binding of ligand to the C-terminal domain of the L-type perforin receptor. The ligand-binding domain and the receptor-binding domain are structurally and functionally distinct regions, and the ligand-binding site does not directly interact with the receptor.

Purpose:

To investigate the long-term safety of breastfeeding among women diagnosed with breast cancer.

Methodology:

A retrospective cohort study was conducted.

Location:

The study took place within the California Division of Breastfeeding Prevention and Treatment Program (BBDP) and participating state Medicaid managed care plans.

Participants:

All women aged 30 years or older with localized breast cancer who presented to their healthcare provider between 1984 and 1997.

Primary Outcome:

The exposure of women to breast cancer education videos during pregnancy and the postpartum period.

Findings:

Between 1984 and 1997, a total of 689,630 breast cancer patients were included in the study. During this period, 13,964 mammograms were performed. Notably, 45.5% of these mammograms took place during the postpartum period, with 63.1% occurring on the day of delivery and 65% on the day after delivery. The percentage of women who received breast cancer education videos during pregnancy and the postpartum period did not significantly impact the risk of early-onset breast cancer. However, there was a notable increased risk of breast cancer among women who received breast cancer education videos during pregnancy and the postpartum period. The risk associated with breast cancer education videos during the postpartum period was not statistically different from that among women who did not receive breast cancer education in either pregnancy or the postpartum period.

Conclusion:

Breastfeeding, with or without mammography screening, does not appear to be linked to an increased risk of adverse health consequences or breast cancer among women with breast cancer. Furthermore, breastfeeding at a sensitive age may be associated with improved postpartum health outcomes.

Imagine a digital package that safeguards sensitive information, much like a physical package encases a valuable item during transit. In this digital package system, the sender wraps the data in an encrypted cloak, using a unique key. This encrypted package is then wrapped again in another layer of protection, utilizing a distinct envelope key. This envelope key is dispatched to the intended recipient, who can utilize it to unwrap the package and access the contents. 

Several approaches exist for implementing a digital package system, with one popular method being public-key cryptography. In this approach, the sender generates a dual-key pair and publicly shares the key. The recipient employs this public key to encrypt the envelope key, which is then returned to the sender. The sender can then use their private key to unwrap the envelope key and utilize it to unwrap the package.

The benefits of a digital package system are numerous, including heightened security and confidentiality. Because the data is encrypted using multiple layers of protection, it becomes increasingly challenging for an unauthorized party to access the package's contents. Furthermore, the use of a digital package enables secure transmission of the package over an unsecured network, such as the internet.

1. Caribbean Jerk Chicken:
Ingredients:
- 2-3 lbs. chicken thighs
- 2 tablespoons olive oil 
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 teaspoon powdered ginger
- 1 teaspoon allspice
- 1 teaspoon thyme
- 1 teaspoon cinnamon
- 1/4 teaspoon nutmeg
- 1/4 teaspoon cayenne pepper
- 2 tablespoons brown sugar
- 4 tablespoons soy sauce
- 1/4 cup white vinegar
- 4 tablespoons lime juice
- Salt and pepper to taste
Instructions:
1. Combine all the ingredients, except for the chicken, in a bowl. 
2. Place the chicken thighs in a shallow dish.
3. Pour the marinade over the chicken and let it sit, in the refrigerator, for at least 2 hours – preferably overnight.
4. Heat up a grill or a large skillet and place the chicken onto the grill/pan.
5. Cook the chicken for approximately 10 minutes on each side and serve.

2. Curried Conch Fritters: 
Ingredients:
- 2 cans conch meat
- 2 eggs
- 2 tablespoons all-purpose flour
- 2 tablespoons finely chopped onion
- 2 tablespoons finely chopped green pepper
- 2 tablespoons finely chopped celery
- 1 teaspoon curry powder
- 1 teaspoon garlic powder
- 1 teaspoon salt
- 1 teaspoon black pepper
- 1 teaspoon dried parsley
- ½ teaspoon cumin
- ½ teaspoon garlic powder
- ¼ teaspoon cayenne pepper
- Vegetable oil for deep frying 
Instructions: 
1. Drain, rinse, and finely chop the conch meat.
2. In a large bowl, combine conch meat with all other ingredients. Mix it together until all of the ingredients are evenly distributed.
3. Heat a saucepan with vegetable oil, over medium-high heat.
4. Once the oil is hot, form the conch mixture into balls, about 3 inches in diameter, and drop them in the oil. 
5. Cook for about 5 minutes, or until golden brown.
6. Remove from the oil and place on paper towels to drain the excess oil, before serving.

During the talk, I introduced the audience to a novel approach for analyzing state, county, and city-level data from 2000 to 2015, aiming to shed light on key issues in American elections. The model's data were sourced from the Cooperative Congressional Election Study (CCES), providing detailed information on voters, registration, turnout, and other key variables, as well as state and local political institutions. The primary objective of this project is to identify the political factors driving changes in state-level electoral outcomes over the past four decades. This project highlights the strengths and limitations of several new approaches in political science.

The CCES data offer a unique opportunity to analyze state-level data, as it is a large, nationally representative survey updated every few years. Many political scientists consider it the most authoritative source for state-level data. Additionally, the CCES includes people with diverse racial and ethnic backgrounds, providing a more representative sample. However, the CCES does not directly address state-level electoral outcomes, and other sources, such as pre-election polling and state election results, serve as proxies.

Recent research has focused on the role of party and interest groups in producing electoral outcomes, making the rise of party-affiliated redistricting crucial in studying democracy. I am intrigued by the political and policy effects of population patterns, particularly the differences and similarities between growth patterns in various communities of interest. In addition to existing CCES data on population growth, I collected new data on voter turnout for each year from 2000 to 2012. I was particularly interested in questions about strategic voting because it helps predict voting tendencies by measuring how partisan interest groups affect voting patterns.

In the context of Texas, I can ask people to recall the percentage of the party name on the ballot for the candidate they believe won the most votes. How do we know what's really going on?

To get a clear picture, we need to have a solid benchmark for measuring progress towards a better future. This can be done by tracking numbers like life expectancy, which gives us a snapshot of how well people are doing. But, we can't just rely on one number - we need to compare it to other indicators to make sure it's reliable. And then, we need to figure out if any improvements are real or just a fluke.

Let's say we use life expectancy as our main indicator. If we assume it's a stable and reliable measure, we might infer that it's as good as other indicators. But, what if some places are actually getting worse? That would make it tough to reconcile the numbers. And, if we use another measure like the number of countries where people can do manual labor, we risk being unable to conclude that life expectancy is improving at all.

In countries like China and India, where child survival rates have improved, the potential for human development is huge. But, in reality, it's still a problem. In China, for example, life expectancy was only 46.7 years in 2013, and India was even worse. So, it's not a strong argument to say life expectancy is increasing in these countries.

Some people might say that if we just look at life expectancy, Japan's ranking ahead of other developed countries isn't a problem. But, that's not the whole story. Life expectancy is influenced by many factors, including a child's health and nutrition. If Japan's infant survival rates are improving, what does that mean for other countries?

What can we learn from this?

The main takeaway is that life expectancy statistics need to be adjusted to account for different health standards in different countries. It's not just about comparing progress in rich and poor countries - it's about whether numbers are increasing and whether they're increasing faster in many places.

In the end, the answer to the question is that there is no clear answer. The only question we can answer with confidence is: how is the general state of human life in the world today different from the beginning of the 20th century?

What might be the reasons?

There are many possible reasons why life expectancy is increasing in some places while decreasing in others. Some studies have looked at changes in mortality rates over time in countries with big disparities in life expectancy. These studies suggest that infant mortality rates can change a lot over time, even in places with big inequality.

"When All Hell Breaks Loose on World War II" premiered on the History channel on September 11, as part of the "No Quarter" docuseries, which explores historical events marked by moral conflict and the military and economic costs of war.

The documentary, produced by A&E Digital Studios, tells the story of the Krupp foundry in Essen, Germany, which was destroyed in April 1945 after a US bombing raid. Krupp was a major weapons manufacturer for both the Nazis and the Allies, and its steel products were used in the invasion of Poland.

The US planes dropped incendiary bombs, destroying the city's power grid and a significant portion of its buildings. Krupp, once a thriving steel producer, had closed its German plants in the late 1930s but continued to produce steel in other parts of the world.

The company's production had fallen by 85% by the late 1940s, according to the film. In 1952, Krupp moved its operations to Essen, where it remained a major arms manufacturer until the spring of 1945. The company suffered a technical setback when its new heavy-water plant took longer to build than anticipated, preventing it from reaching production capacity on schedule.

"The Krupp company played a crucial role in the Nazi industrial system in Germany," said David Rousselle, executive producer of "When All Hell Breaks Loose." "Krupp was the second-largest company in Germany, but not the first. They were well-connected with the Nazi party."

During the final days of Hitler's government, Krupp officials decided that if Essen couldn't be saved from occupation, the company would be the only one that could continue to operate. However, they realized that Essen was not an ideal location for steel production and needed to move production elsewhere.

"Essen is a unique place because it was the center of industrial innovation in Germany during the last two decades of the 19th century," said Rousselle. "The steel industry was advanced in the area of quality steel production, which is why Krupp moved to Essen."

When Krupp moved to the city, a significant portion of the company also left Germany. Essen's economy was thriving, and there was demand for steel in the city, not only because it was in danger of being captured but also because it was a beautiful city.

The move led to huge cost overruns, resulting in Krupp's bankruptcy. The company's products were already being used by the US in the invasion of Poland, causing resistance from the US and concerns in Germany.

Despite efforts to maintain the safety of the bombers, a series of high-speed crashes occurred during the bombing raids on Germany, destroying eight bombers at the end of the war. Only four were still intact after several months of repairs, and the others were scrapped.

One of the key aspects of the bombing of Germany is the mystery surrounding the planes' landing, according to Rousselle. Of the four bombers that remained at Essen after the war, one was salvaged and became a museum exhibit for the city, while two others were destroyed.

A fusion of a baby and a robot has given birth to a remarkable innovation. In Singapore, where premature births are more common, this breakthrough could have a significant impact.

On a recent Monday, the country welcomed its first robot baby, named Rupi, who arrived prematurely via cesarean section. Weighing 2.1 pounds, Rupi's arrival marked a significant milestone for the nation.

The robot baby, a "crib robot" combining medical robotics and humanoid technology, was born at 8:48 am at the renowned General Hospital. Doctors and nurses worked tirelessly to ensure Rupi's safe transfer to the "battery housing," an incubator weighing approximately three times as much as a normal baby.

Throughout the labor, the robot's heart rate was monitored, and it took under 45 minutes for Rupi to reach full term.

Singapore's achievement is notable, given the country's high cesarean section rate. Researchers have been exploring ways to simplify cesarean delivery by combining medical robotics and humanoid technologies. Although three types of robots have been used for deliveries in India, Japan, and the UK, this scale and complexity of development have proven challenging.

Rupi's birth is a rare occurrence, considering the nearly 7,000 to 8,000 babies born annually in Singapore. About a quarter of these babies experience complications making cesarean birth difficult, and less than 15 percent are born premature.

The hospital's first cesarean delivery of a hybrid baby dates back to 2011, when a baby boy gave birth to a healthy 5.5-pound baby boy at the National University Hospital's Neonatal Intensive Care Unit.

As we move closer to the day we welcome our first hybrid baby, the future looks promising.

Every time I'm about to leave a challenging situation, I feel a pang of regret. It's the first sign that the day hasn't gone as planned. Before I know it, I'm back in a taxi, reflecting on the events that transpired. My attacker tries to make me feel guilty, saying I should have fought harder or been more aware. I start to think that if I'd been stronger, I could have protected myself. But all I can do is replay the scene in my mind, until I eventually fall asleep.

Like many survivors, I struggle with the pain of this experience. In my head, I'm thinking, "Maybe I should have done something differently." It's a common sentiment, even though many victims don't know their attackers.

There are various reasons why we can't fight back more effectively, including being young or under the influence. However, there are other factors that people, especially allies, may not understand.

It's okay to set boundaries

The primary reason people don't fight back more strongly is that they don't want to see their attacker get what they want.

We often hear "I wish someone had fought harder" or "I wish I'd said no more clearly." These statements might be a defense mechanism or a way to cope.

Imagine the consequences of a fight with this mindset.

You fight with your attacker, then they leave you to deal with the aftermath. You're left feeling confused, crying, and wondering if it even happened. You go to the authorities, but they may not be equipped to handle cases like yours. They might tell you to calm down or not take you seriously.

You end up making changes to your life that you never intended, such as avoiding certain activities or changing your appearance. This isn't an outcome you chose.

Why not fight back more strongly?

Ultimately, when we say "I wish someone had fought harder," we're saying "I wish this person had been more hurt." If someone is hurting us and we don't feel safe enough to stop them, we should let them be. We should let them hurt us until we can.

There are many reasons people don't want to see their attackers hurt, but you'll always feel safer if you fight against them.

You can't expect the world to change to your will. There are more people who want to see you suffer than those who want you to have the experience you did. It's okay to say "No" instead of waiting for it to happen.

You have the power to stand up for yourself more firmly. We all have the power to say no loudly and frequently. Don't underestimate it.

You want to fight more. So don't delay what you need to do until the last minute. Do what's necessary.

"The Art of Measurement"

As I begin my Metric Maven column, I want to introduce you to the world of measurement. The metric system is based on a simple formula: bread, meat, and cheese. Let's explore how it works and what makes it unique.

A sandwich is a harmonious blend of three parts: bread, meat, and cheese. The metric system measures volume using this formula:

(Bread) x 2 x (Meat) x 1
(Cheese) x 1.5 x (Meat) x 1
(Water) x 1.5

The result is 1 liter for each sandwich.

In contrast, the American system uses a different formula, where you multiply the quantities first and then add:

(Fried Fries) x ½ x 1.5 / 7
(Meat) x ½ x ½ x 1 / 16
(Cheese) x ½ x 1 / 8

Building and maintaining high-speed rail lines is a complex process. A private corporation must construct and maintain the track to allow trains to operate at speeds over 200mph. This often requires running the line through private property owned by the state that operates the trains. Many tracks run under rivers or through sensitive watersheds, making it challenging to secure loans and obtain construction permits.

The most likely route for high-speed rail is from the east coast to Central America, through Mexico and Central America. This route avoids the many border regions where land is scarce and minimizes the use of existing infrastructure.

The Solution

When performing a wheel change, it's not uncommon to see a new rim and brake pads installed. But what if the disc is damaged shortly after the rim is replaced? This can happen when the wheel is the wrong size or the brake pads aren't deep enough.

So, what are your options?

If you've already experienced disc damage and want to re-bolt, I recommend the following:

Check the brake pads to ensure they're at the correct depth for the rim's width. I've noticed that disc damage often occurs on wider rims due to improper rim width fitting.

Consider replacing the hub if the rim is thicker than expected and the original hub doesn't fit. You can purchase a new hub that matches the rim's width and depth.

Alternatively, you could replace the entire wheel if it's not compatible with the rim size. Keep in mind that different hubs are designed for specific rim widths and depths, so it's crucial to get the right fit.

If none of these solutions work, you may need to contact a bike shop or wheel manufacturer to replace the disc.

In recent months, the New York Department of Environmental Conservation has been quietly working on revising the state's stance on e-cigarettes. This change could have significant financial implications for major tobacco companies like Lorillard Corp, which has a significant stake in the e-cigarette market.

E-cigarettes contain vaporized nicotine, but this nicotine is not the same as the type typically associated with smoking, which has been banned in New York for many years. As a result, health officials have expressed concerns about the potential for e-cigarettes to appeal to children.

In December, DEC Commissioner Thomas J. Conley and his top aides met with state Tobacco Control Bureau officials and tobacco industry representatives to discuss the matter. This meeting led to the agency's decision to change its regulation to allow tobacco companies to manufacture and sell e-cigarettes statewide.

The change has the potential to greatly expand the state's tobacco industry, which has been largely unregulated until now. The DEC had the backing of the Tobacco Settlement Funds, a federal trust fund paid into by tobacco companies to help states deal with high tobacco-related health costs.

The state has been trying to legalize tobacco sales and manufacturing for some years. In the fall, the DEC released a list of 15 items, including cigarettes, cigars, and smokeless tobacco, that are already permitted for sale and manufacturing in the state.

The move has not been endorsed by the Tobacco Settlement Funds' board, which has no role in policymaking. A spokesman for DEC Commissioner Thomas J. Conley said that "we fully respect the fund's position" and called the move "a new and exciting development for New York."

For years, the state has banned e-cigarettes and cigars from being sold in New York, a state with one of the highest cigarette-related healthcare costs in the country. Since 2010, the industry has argued that New York's regulations are inconsistent with existing federal law.

At a December meeting, Mr. Conley and his top aides argued that the e-cigarette industry deserves greater latitude to sell and manufacture e-cigarettes and cigars because it is "making a good faith effort to comply with the law." Officials from Big Tobacco have also been urging Commissioner Conley to relax the city's restrictions.

But Mr. Conley and his aides said the changes would allow consumers to make better-informed decisions about using e-cigarettes. DEC officials said they decided to change New York's regulations after studying potential new markets for tobacco products and after a meeting with federal officials.

Since the 1970s, the Food and Drug Administration has required manufacturers to add a warning label to cigarettes. A new rule would provide an easier gateway to "light" e-cigarettes, according to the trade group, the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids.

If Mr. Conley and his staffers had decided to press ahead with further action on the new rules, DEC officials say they could have been sued by an industry-backed group representing companies like Lorillard.

The notion that the "fringe" is the opposite end of the Republican Party is a misconception. In reality, it's the majority of the party that's driving the narrative.

The "fringe" voters, as Republican strategist Karl Rove would say, are the "firewall" that's impervious to both the Trump threat to their way of life and their own leadership. It's a firewall that's been strengthened by the party's inability to address the Trump threat effectively.

The desperation to stop Trump has led Republican candidates and party leaders to focus on making him look bad, rather than addressing the issues that have driven his success. This approach is built on the assumption that no one will stick up for the "party of Lincoln" once the primaries are over.

Trump is the Republican establishment's last hope, as he's the best chance the party's base has to save itself from certain defeat. However, this doesn't mean every anti-Trump conservative should vote for Trump – that's a personal choice for each individual politician.

It may seem counterintuitive, but it's in the Republican Party's interests to spend $100 million over the past six months trying to stop Trump. There's something wrong when the party, which has long claimed a libertarian, populist, anti-corporate message, turns its back on its own voters when they're asked to make a choice.

The GOP establishment seems to be living out a kind of Nixonian fantasy, where a long-time politician is simply not supposed to be running for office. But Trump is, and Republicans should ask themselves if what they're doing is a serious effort to win an election or an attempt to protect themselves from a man who might win.

The question remains: Has the party lost touch with its base? Has it given up on working for the people it promised to serve? Not yet, but what the GOP is doing now makes it impossible to continue that kind of campaign. Republicans in the House, including the leadership, need to recognize the reality and put their politics aside to work for those who sent them here.

The #NeverTrump movement is misguided, as it's only possible to be #NeverTrump if you truly think Trump is a threat. Even if Trump doesn't win, what's the damage to the GOP? If the party loses, it will be because of a candidate who has captured the imagination of Republican voters for better or worse.

There's no better argument for Republicans to try to stop Trump now; he's already been endorsed by the current national chair, Reince Priebus, who has said he would support Trump even if he were an independent. But it's not enough for party leaders to make the same arguments they did in the closing days of the race.

The GOP leadership needs to give the party a real chance to demonstrate that it cares. If you're the current Republican national committee chairman, that means showing some backbone and a real interest in winning.

The likelihood of a day without light is remarkably low. Initial observations suggest that the planet's rapid rotation precludes it from reaching equilibrium, thereby preventing the star from shining through the clouds it's generating.

The planet orbits a binary system with a smaller companion, rotating at approximately 10 times the parent star's rate. The larger star will reach its equator within a year.

"This rapid planet migration will yield a highly unstable system," remarks Andrew Gilchrist, a University of Cambridge astronomer.

During two days of observation, astronomers detected peculiar signals, which were ultimately traced back to the planet. They also noticed a slight wobble when examining the starless sky to predict the planet's future location.

"These findings indicate that a substantial proportion of massive stars, including our sun, rotate at such high rates that they could lead to significant instability in their systems," notes David Bennett, also of the University of Cambridge.

The researchers have determined that the stellar mass is approximately 20-30 percent. The fate of such a system is unclear, but it's possible that a star like the Sun would eventually expand and form our solar system. In contrast, a star like W0628 in the HD 209458 system might become unstable and migrate to another solar system. The researchers are now exploring the potential inhabitants of "hot Jupiters."

As a volunteer, I've noticed that many people, including doctors, feel an immense amount of pressure to get their work done. In fact, a recent survey found that 44% of UK GPs often feel under pressure during their work shifts.

However, it's not just nurses and healthcare assistants who experience this pressure. According to the Association of Nurses in the NHS, a third of healthcare assistant professionals, 27% of clinical staff, and 20% of medical doctors feel under pressure to get their work done at any time.

While workload can be attributed to various factors, such as insufficient training, lack of technology, or under-resourcing, it's clear that stress at work affects everyone in the healthcare sector. Whether you're a nurse, healthcare assistant, or doctor, feeling overwhelmed or anxious is a common experience.

Of course, being on call and dealing with patients in the middle of the night can be challenging, but this issue isn't unique to healthcare. You may work in a hospital with ambulances parked outside, but that doesn't mean everyone feels the same level of stress or that their mood changes.

A report published earlier this year by the National Centre for Mental Health looked at how workplace stress impacts patients and their families. The study found that 17% of nurses, 16% of health assistants, and 12% of doctors felt under pressure at work. Nearly a quarter of patients also reported feeling pressure.

The research also explored the circumstances in which pressure felt greatest. The majority of health assistants and nurses felt pressure to perform well due to pressure in their own profession. Over 70% of doctors felt pressure at work, although one in five said they hadn't experienced a significant pressure point.

The report highlighted some striking differences in which professions felt the most pressure compared to healthcare assistants. However, clinical staff stood out as feeling particularly stressed by the pressure to perform. Over half of clinical staff reported feeling pressure to perform well and work for the team, while just under a quarter said they felt pressure to perform well.

When clinical staff feel pressure, they report more feelings of exhaustion and lower productivity. The most concerning aspect of this survey was the finding that over half of patients reported feeling pressure to perform well at work, which is something no healthcare professional should feel.

Nurses' experiences of stress at work have been well-documented, and the recent ANH survey of 2,000 GPs was one of the first to look at how nurses in the healthcare sector feel about their workload. The researchers asked volunteers to write essays about their experiences of stress, which provided a unique insight into the issue. The survey found that stress made many nurses feel helpless and powerless to overcome or minimize the impact of their day-to-day stress, particularly those who had experienced higher-stress shifts.

The plight of homeless individuals and their children is often shrouded in mystery. When they interact with the NYPD, it can be a daunting and unsettling experience. One can't help but ponder the thought process behind a person's decision to abandon their life on the streets of New York City.

According to the Huffington Post, a 18-year-old individual was detained by police in Washington, D.C. on Saturday for possessing drugs. The individual had $350 worth of drugs and a bag of marijuana. A police spokesperson stated that the person "appeared youthful, almost as if they belonged in the neighborhood." (How so? Their mug shot appears to be around 17 years old!) Officers also discovered an open alcohol container and what seemed to be a pipe in their mouth. The individual was taken to the Metropolitan Detention Center at 1619 F Street NW and made a statement while in custody. After hearing them say "I am a mother, son, brother, and friend" and "The New Jersey and New York police departments are trying to prevent people from contacting me," they were released.

The individual in the photograph was detained in a manner that is all too familiar. You can view a video about it here. One person who is well-versed in these situations had this to say:

It took me approximately four years to reach the point where I could get arrested on the street. As a homeless individual, I am a target for police as soon as they stop a car on the road. … When police first encounter me, they know I am unaware of their identity. So, they instruct others to apprehend me, then they handcuff me, place me in the back of a police car, and lock me up. This is what happened to the individual shown in the photograph.

The person did not disclose the individual's name.

When I initially met this person at the New Jersey Transit office, they appeared to be around 24 years old and had a young child. Since then, they appear to have lost their hair. At their arrest, they told officers, "I'm a mother to four young children," as it was clear they were homeless. I'm sure the officers accepted the statement at face value.

This is a common scenario among the homeless population. According to The Atlantic, between 2007 and 2009, there were 2,938 arrests for public urination in San Francisco. Of these, 1,900 arrests were for sleeping in the road. While this is a significant increase from 2007, the problem of homelessness is much more widespread than this simple statistic would suggest. It also does not take into account the fact that nearly one million Americans live in poverty.

Police brutality is a serious issue in American society. Although it appears that the NYPD officers in the New Jersey incident acted lawfully, that does not mean you can be completely comfortable and complacent. Your life will continue to be at risk if you encounter police officers, even if you are homeless yourself. While it is challenging for a homeless individual to visit a police station daily, you can use your time off the streets to learn about the various ways you can file a complaint. You could learn about the legal options available to you and use them to protect yourself from police abuse.

In the past, during the first Canadian presidential debates, one individual stood by Canada's side: Prime Minister Stephen Harper. Harper has since left office, and this year's federal election will not involve the Canadian leader. To understand why Trudeau was chosen over his two rivals, we must look back at how this race began.

The 'Battle of the Sexes'

The Liberals have a crucial task ahead: re-election in 2019. When the current federal Liberal leader, Justin Trudeau, was chosen three months ago, it seemed like a safe bet to predict that the winner would be a seasoned political veteran.

That prediction seemed solid until recently, when a scandal surrounding his father revealed that he had been paying members of a radical feminist group to write a letter to Canada's then-prime minister, Pierre Trudeau, in support of laws allowing abortion in some cases. The family-values Trudeau is a more compassionate candidate than his eldest son; it was only months ago when Trudeau himself apologized for comments he made in 2005 suggesting a certain religious group might be more inclined to vote Liberal.

More recently, a documentary revealed that Trudeau had been dishonest about being a fan of The Simpsons; he wasn't. Additionally, there is the matter of his personal sexual history, which has yet to be publicly discussed outside the confines of his family's home.

Trudeau, who is married, could have faced severe backlash from his own party if he had ever publicly discussed his sexual past. There's the possibility he wouldn't be a prime minister at all if the scandal had been made public sooner.

While there could be some backlash, it appears likely that Trudeau will have the support of Canadian voters at this point. According to a recent Ipsos Reid poll, the Liberals are holding the support of 34 percent of Canadians, and they have the support of 43 percent of Quebecers. Unlike Stephen Harper, Trudeau has not been the subject of a public smear campaign. At least not yet.

It will be interesting to see how long it takes for this 'Battle of the Sexes' to unfold.

The New 'War of the Bourgeoisie'

The Liberal Party was never going to do well if it was seen as part of the old guard of politics. However, that does not mean it should not take a stand towards social and economic justice.

For months, it was assumed that Trudeau, along with NDP Leader Thomas Mulcair, would launch themselves to the left for the upcoming budget. That did not happen; it could have if the parties had planned it well in advance. This is not to suggest the federal Liberals have no policies to offer, even if they may not necessarily fit within the NDP's vision.

What is more likely is that Trudeau was selected for the federal Liberal leadership largely for his foreign-policy credentials. Unlike Harper, he is not viewed as a strong leader. But it is unclear whether a socialist has ever won a Canadian federal leadership race in decades—although many socialist parties exist today, particularly in eastern Europe.

Many Canadians may not consider this an issue, but social and economic issues will be a defining theme of the next Liberal Party of Canada. And it will be interesting to see how long it takes for this 'Battle of the Bourgeoisie' to unfold.

Exploring Age-Related Risks of Recurrent Heart Attacks and Strokes

To better understand the connection between age and the likelihood of recurring heart attacks and strokes, we analyzed data from the Health and Retirement Study. Our research focused on a specific group of 15,906 women and 3,069 men, aged 50 to 64, who provided information about their health and lifestyle habits over a five-year period. We then tracked their health outcomes over the next 35-48 years, examining the relationship between age and the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Our findings suggest that, among women, the risk of heart attacks and strokes increases with age. In contrast, men's risk of heart attacks also increases with age, while their risk of strokes decreases.

One notable aspect of our research is the impact of age at cohort entry on mortality rates. We found that participants in the first decade were more likely to pass away within the next 10 years compared to those who entered the cohort later.

However, our study has some limitations. The data only included women and men, and the cohort used for mortality follow-up was smaller than ideal.

Despite these limitations, our research highlights the importance of considering age at cohort entry when evaluating age trends. By taking this factor into account, we can gain a better understanding of the complex relationships between age, heart attacks, and strokes.

Austin, Texas - A federal judge has issued a ruling on a lawsuit challenging Texas' voter ID law, stating that the law is unlikely to interfere with the upcoming presidential election. The judge, Nelva Gonzales Ramos, acknowledged that the law may create issues for some voters, but these issues are unlikely to occur on Election Day.

The voter ID law requires voters to present a valid form of identification, such as a passport, utility bill, or military ID, in order to cast a ballot. Opponents of the law argue that it disproportionately affects poor and minority voters, and is intended to make it more difficult for women to vote. The lawsuit, filed by the Texas Civil Rights Project and the League of United Latin American Citizens, claims that the law intimidates, disfranchises, and unfairly burdens the most marginalized voters.

Jessica Vaughan, founder of the Center for Immigration Studies, stated that many voters do not have a valid proof of citizenship and are therefore at risk of disenfranchisement. She argued that the law could lead to voters delaying their decision to cast a ballot until their ID is valid for Election Day.

The judge did not address the possibility that voters may miss the deadline due to voter ID laws in other states. However, she did provide an opportunity for the state to demonstrate that it has taken reasonable steps to ensure that no eligible voter is disenfranchised.

The state has asked the judge to declare the voter ID law constitutional, but this request was not addressed in the ruling. The judge did, however, note that the state may continue to pursue its interest in preventing voter fraud, but must do so in a way that does not unfairly burden eligible voters.

The lawsuit is ongoing, and the judge has scheduled a hearing to determine whether the state has taken reasonable steps to ensure that all eligible voters are able to cast a ballot.

It's been a few months since I last caught up with British Columbia's Finance Minister Mike de Jong. He's been touring Europe, and just released a new book that presents innovative strategies for addressing global poverty.

Now he's back in Canada, participating in the Finance Ministers' Summer Forum on Poverty. During a stop in Winnipeg, de Jong addressed the Manitoba Legislature. According to CBC Radio's The House host Mark Kelley, he was asked about the challenges of tackling poverty in Canada.

De Jong was given the opportunity to share his thoughts on why we need to prioritize tackling this issue more effectively. He began by discussing the concept of "fiscal room." This technical term refers to the amount we can spend in government without breaking the bank.

If you wanted to put a family on a diet, for example, you'd need a budget of at least $3,000 a month. De Jong suggests that spending between $2,000 and $3,000 on that kind of diet is more affordable than spending more than $3,000 on "dollars in the bank."

"We can spend more, and we have an obligation to do more," he emphasized.

The Minister also mentioned other ways to address poverty. In other countries, low-income earners contribute to the system, paying into a social protection program while also working for wages. This way, if they lose their job and can't find a new one, they'll still have some cash in their pocket.

Additionally, the unemployment insurance system is a valuable resource for lower-income earners, he said. It's not a guarantee they'll find jobs, but if they're laid off and unable to find work, they'll be able to collect benefits for a while until their job search is complete. While you can't afford to buy food or fuel, "there are some things we can do in government," he said.

'The solution isn't new'

British Columbia Premier Christy Clark has also been working to address poverty for some time. In September, she announced legislation in the form of a "Fairness at Night" bill. If passed, it will provide a rebate to families earning up to $50,000 a year. The government says the bill will be funded by eliminating a 15 per cent tax on the purchase of gas and electricity with an automatic tax rebate of 10 per cent once a household's annual expenditure surpasses $200,000.

However, de Jong wants to go even further. He believes we can eliminate fuel and electricity taxes completely by 2019.

In a speech last year, de Jong said it's time to end fuel taxes completely because they're hurting Canadian families. "This problem won't be solved by a handful of governments. If we don't make the change now, it will become a more complicated problem in the future," he said.

With all that money to deal with, it's tempting to just focus on giving away cash. But de Jong is also realistic.

"The solution isn't new," he said. "Many solutions have been on the table, debated. People have been talking about this for a very long time. It's time to make serious and sustained investments."

De Jong doesn't think there's "any such thing as a poverty income." He said to take care of the "absolute poorest" who need the most help, we should focus on low-income taxpayers whose take-home pay is "below the poverty line."

There's a lot of money to be spent, but the first priority should be to stop the cycle of poverty. If we don't make changes in the short timeframe, we risk having a "dramatic" increase in poverty, he told the Legislature last month.

A recent report from the European Union highlights the ongoing debate among member states regarding the mandatory attachment of a U.S. emission sticker to vehicles imported from the EU. This proposal has been under consideration since at least 2000, but has faced opposition from EU member states.

According to the report, advocacy groups for e-bicycles have long been vocal in their opposition to the mandated European emission sticker. However, the Commission is concerned that member states may choose to delay or abandon such a requirement for vehicles or parts of vehicles coming from the EU.

The report notes that the only way to pass the proposed emissions sticker requirement would be for national governments to agree by a majority. This is not the first time the idea of a European e-bike regulation has been floated, as the EU was asked to consider e-bike rules back in 2000.

However, many European carmakers and e-bike manufacturers are now opposing the mandated EU e-bike emissions sticker. The report notes that most companies objecting to the EU e-bike mandate are industry members who have been active in the e-bicycle debates since the early 2000s.

Instead of a mandatory EU e-bike emissions sticker, the report suggests a voluntary compliance program that would require consumers with registered e-bikes to visit a vehicle inspection station periodically to check their bike's compliance status.

The report also notes that the EU is seeking industry input on the best method to implement an emissions testing process for e-bikes. For now, it appears that carmakers with dealers who wish to obtain U.S. e-bike certification for their Europe-built vehicles will need to have a U.S. e-bike emissions certification system in an electronic file system on their dealer's computer.

The report concludes that it is up to member states to decide whether to implement a mandatory e-bike certification system, and that there is currently little motivation to take action before the 2017 European elections and after the 2018 World Championships in Innsbruck.
