The University of Toronto is embarking on a significant transformation. By elevating its flagship medical school to the top ten globally, it has established a bold new program that will add a new faculty and create 30 new post-secondary positions by 2020. Additionally, the institution has implemented a policy capping funding for graduate students, who currently comprise approximately 40% of U of T's undergraduate population.

This shift is not unprecedented, as many Canadian universities have undergone changes in recent years. "When I was a student in Canada, I recall that we used to play 'c' for certain classes," says Chris Hadfield, author of the Canadian university guide, Universities of the World. "It didn't mean you couldn't take the class; it simply meant they wouldn't pay you. That's no longer the case."

Undergraduate enrollment has reached its highest level since 1966, with a 6.6% increase from 2014. Moreover, enrollment is up at universities ranked higher than U of T's, with students from 33 countries and territories attending in 2015.

While the Canadian system has its strengths, it also faces notable challenges. "Universities are financed in a system where there are winners and losers, where the university that receives a grant attracts many students, and others receive a lower share of funding," notes Hadfield, who founded a network of post-secondary and private universities with high enrollment.

The Canadian system has undergone significant changes since its inception. In the mid-1970s, when U of T was established, public funding was set aside as provincial university funding to support the "first-tier system." At the time, there were concerns about the long-term sustainability of public universities in the post-secondary era.

Canada has transitioned from having the largest student population and number of students to being one of the least-funded nations on earth. "When discussing Canadian universities, we should be concerned about the insufficient public funding for them in Canada, which is unable to meet the demand of the student population," says Hadfield.

If students pay more for higher education, the funds can be targeted at improving access, increasing efficiency, and enhancing quality. "We're not conducting the kind of research and funding that would support our capacity to be a national university system."

The key difference is that U of T will utilize funding raised through enrollment to provide a more generous grant compared to other Canadian universities. For instance, in 2012-13, U of T raised 6.5% of undergraduate tuition revenue through tuition and fees, a rate more than double that of Quebec's Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec, the country's second-largest university system. In contrast, Canada's overall university grant system provides grants for 5% or less of tuition.

This is in stark contrast to the U.S., which awards grants to more than 60% of student tuition through its federal student assistance program, also providing funds to private schools. This program has had a significant impact on U of T, allowing it to increase academic and research spending, as well as the share of total costs it pays in operating grants.

However, the increase in funding at U of T means higher costs and a greater investment in infrastructure. "A third of U of T's operating costs are directly related to capital costs of building."

In a recent report on what's needed to keep universities competitive in an increasingly competitive global economy, Hadfield advocated for a "different approach" to university funding.

A verdict has been reached in the trial of an Israeli soldier accused of being involved in the deaths of three Palestinian children. The soldier, identified as 31-year-old Corporal Ofer Trope, was acquitted of all charges related to the incident.

According to reports, Trope was driving in the occupied West Bank when his vehicle was damaged during a stone-throwing incident. In response, he allegedly fired into a passing car, resulting in the deaths of the three children.

The military court indicted Trope on two counts of murder, but he was ultimately convicted of manslaughter and homicide. During questioning, Trope admitted that his actions were not reasonable and did not align with the high moral values of the Israeli army.

The verdict has sparked controversy, with some Israeli officials expressing concerns that the army has not done enough to address the frequent violence that erupts during mass protests staged by Palestinians. Critics have also accused Israel of being slow to act to quell unrest.

The incident occurred during a period of heightened tension in the region, following the killing of a teenager during clashes between Israelis and Palestinians on a Jerusalem street.

Trope's sister initially sought a pardon for her brother, but later withdrew her request. The army's disciplinary authority has recommended dismissal for Trope, citing his "flagrant disregard for the safety of soldiers."

A recent $60 billion settlement between the Justice Department and civil rights groups has sparked controversy over a plan aimed at preventing potentially fraudulent institutions from accessing the banking system. Dubbed Operation Choke Point, the initiative involves the largest banks, including Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Citigroup, and JP Morgan Chase, agreeing to reforms.

Critics argue that the plan undermines the free market by regulating and limiting what banks can do in making risky loans. However, the Justice Department and civil rights groups insist it doesn't amount to a "choke point" in the financial market.

The plan doesn't require banks to stop loan modifications, but instead, they'll report data on their lending performance. Deputy Attorney General James Cole emphasized that it's not a policy, and there will be various ways to achieve the goal.

Operation Choke Point began in May 2012, initially aimed at restricting banks' internal lending rates. In March, the government settled with 27 financial institutions, collectively managing over $40 billion in assets.

The plan has been widely criticized by consumer groups and lawmakers, who argue it's an attempt to create a policy, not a "choke point." Justice officials believe it's not their responsibility to impose restrictions on big banks.

Some banks have expressed concerns, with Bank of America stating it's committed to its business relationship with the government and remains committed to serving clients, customers, and communities.

The plan's controversial nature is evident, with experts like Robert McChesney, a law professor at the University of Florida, questioning its business sense. He believes it's a way for the Justice Department to avoid accountability and impose restrictions on banks without congressional approval.

The proposal is awaiting approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and will require banks to report loan quality data. If the department discovers material issues, it can initiate a review to determine if the bank is satisfactory in its treatment of individuals. If the bank disagrees with the findings, it can appeal to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

The plan aims to give the government control over whether banks can make risky loans without putting themselves at risk.

The NCAA's football postseason ban for three years and a lifetime ban for any associate football coach took effect immediately, with retroactive application, the organization announced on Monday.

The sanctions have left the Big Ten without a postseason game for the third consecutive season, following penalties in 2010 for academic issues. As a result, Ohio State and Miami will not be participating in postseason competitions.

Ohio State is scheduled to play Virginia Tech in the Fiesta Bowl on December 31 and will now have the opportunity to select its quarterbacks for the upcoming season.

Big Ten Conference President Jim Delany emphasized the importance of moving forward, stating, "We can't change the past, but we can work towards a brighter future."

Ohio State Athletic Director Gene Smith praised the Big Ten's members for their courage in addressing the issue, saying, "The Big Ten's members demonstrated moral courage by holding those accountable who did wrong."

Tomblin also highlighted the significance of the Ohio State-Michigan rivalry, noting that it has become more important than ever to the university.

The sanctions mark the latest development in a long-standing NCAA investigation involving allegations of wrongdoing at Ohio State.

The university was previously penalized for its lack of a full-time compliance official, recruiting violations, and failure to report a potential relationship between a booster and an NCAA official.

The NCAA imposed a nine-year postseason ban and a $40 million fine on Penn State, as well as an 18-year postseason ban that will begin after the 2015 season, and a lifetime ban for any football coach who was an assistant.

The organization also prohibited Penn State and its employees from recruiting the son of former football assistant coach Jerry Sandusky and banned head coach James Franklin for two years, along with all six of his football assistants.

The NCAA's findings included the lack of a child abuse prevention program at Penn State, and the failure of university officials to report abuse allegations during the time Jerry Sandusky was employed.

We've curated a list of 15 notable non-chain eateries in and around Washington, DC, categorized by cuisine such as French, Italian, Asian, Italian-American, seafood, comfort food, and barbecue. This way, you can focus on discovering new flavors. Although some of these establishments may be located outside of DC, it's still possible to visit and enjoy their offerings. For a more comprehensive list, please click the provided link.

1. Bouchon (1923 Connecticut Ave NW)

This charming eatery boasts an old-world ambiance and minimal frills. The food is exceptional, and the patio or bar area is perfect for a relaxing drink. Although primarily catering to French-speaking clientele, the staff is accommodating to English-speaking patrons and willing to accept French payment. Bouchon is an excellent choice for group dining, as everyone is sure to appreciate the cuisine. The restaurant's history dates back to its former life as a sushi bar, but its current incarnation is a welcome change.

2. The Blue Duck

Located adjacent to Bouchon, The Blue Duck is often considered a single entity. The menu is relatively straightforward, but the food is satisfying. As the oldest establishment on this list, dating back to 1912, it's a testament to its enduring popularity. While the menu is limited, the signature burger is a must-try, and the full meal option is a great value.

3. L'Espalier (2150 Connecticut Ave NW)

This understated gem boasts small, cozy rooms that don't feel cramped. The old-school atmosphere is enhanced by its seafood offerings and filling burgers. Located in a residential neighborhood, it's an ideal spot for a quick bite or a leisurely meal.

4. La Ristorante Italiano (1700 18th St NW)

This beloved eatery was a favorite haunt of President John F. Kennedy, situated in the heart of DC. While not a high-end establishment, it offers good value with affordable meals. The menu features a range of options, with steak and lasagna being the main attractions.

5. D'Andrea's Ristorante Italiano (1310 N 17th St NW)

This historic mansion-turned-restaurant is owned by an Italian family, who have lived in the house and operated the restaurant since the 16th century. The menu is largely unchanged, but prices are slightly higher. While the food is excellent, the prices may not justify the cost.

6. Borsch (2930 Irving St NW)

Located in the same neighborhood as Bouchon, Borsch is one of the oldest restaurants in DC. Unfortunately, it's only open for dinner, and the menu is limited. However, the staff is friendly, and it's a great spot for takeout when reservations are unavailable. We enjoyed the Chicken Parmigiana, which came with a delightful herb pesto and cheese enchiladas.

7. Vino (2900 Irving St NW)

This eclectic eatery, situated next to Bouchon, offers a diverse menu. While the food is good, it may not live up to its reputation due to its prime location. If you're in the area and craving a hearty meal, Vino is a reliable option.

8. Aperitivo Italiano (3813 K Street NW)

This modern Italian restaurant features a fresh menu in a casual setting. The food is good, but not exceptional, and the prices are reasonable. Despite being a new establishment, Aperitivo has built a loyal following and is a popular spot for locals and visitors alike.

The cause of the derailment remains under investigation. Amtrak released a statement expressing their concern for those involved and promising to provide updates as more information becomes available.

NJ Transportation Authority officials confirmed that three cars were involved in the incident and that an engine fire occurred. The fire department battled the blaze, and the cause of the fire is still unknown.

A federal law enforcement official noted that the fire appeared to be isolated, but it's unclear whether it was caused by the crash or if it was a deliberate act.

A coalition of advocates is taking a stand against Google, urging the tech giant to remove an image of a Palestinian child being severely injured in its search results.

Palestinian rights organizations claim that images of the tragic demise of a five-year-old Palestinian boy from Kawareneh, a village near Ramallah in the West Bank, can potentially trigger hostility towards Israeli citizens.

A representative for the Middle East Children's Alliance, Saima Abdullah, told Al Jazeera that the image "incites animosity and promotion of hatred towards Israeli citizens".

"This was a deliberate decision by the Israeli company [iGoogle] to be complicit with the Israeli government and promotion in our name.

"It's not only insulting the Palestinian people, it's insulting the Palestinian government which has been striving to combat racism and to bring peace to the Middle East. They're helping promote this hateful image."

Abdullah, who is also an IT teacher, has created a petition on change.org titled "Google to Remove The image of 5 year-old Mohammed being severely injured on their search results." The petition currently has over 2,500 supporters.

It has been signed by former Palestinian president and current secretary-general of the PLO, Saeb Erekat, among others.

"We believe that we will see a lot more petitions and complaints, as there's a lot of frustration among the Palestinian people about this," said Abdullah.

Google denied the allegations of promotion. "We have already taken legal action against some Palestinian online forums over this issue. We encourage the Palestinian communities to take the matter to court rather than to use legal methods," said a spokesperson for iGoogle who spoke to Al Jazeera on the condition of anonymity.

Image copyright iGoogle Image caption Google says the images were posted on a Palestinian forum


"The image was posted on a Palestinian forum and our employees did nothing wrong. The images are also not offensive in every way, but it is a clear violation of Google's guidelines, and a violation of the company's policies, to link to them on our website.

"We have contacted the Israeli authorities about this. The Palestinian Authority and Google will be working together to address this issue. It is our policy not to moderate content or hide from the issue."

Since its formation in 2012, the Middle East Children's Alliance has been working with Palestinian authorities to bring about social change in the region, said Abdullah.

"For example, we've helped teach our children to say 'no' to adults.

"We do this by teaching our children to fight for themselves, to stand up for their rights and to fight for their future. We're very proud of how we have done this to our kids, and of their example."

Although most of his students are male, Abdullah said that he would teach his female students to learn how to get organized, to be strong and to do what is right.

"When my students talk to me, they tell me that they want to run to become leaders, to become teachers and to become activists. They are inspiring me. These are the children of Palestine who inspire us."

Abdullah has set up a YouTube channel aimed at helping his pupils become informed.

OK Cupid, the world's most popular dating app, has been experimenting with innovative technology and has successfully integrated it into some of its new games. One of these games allows users to match with others based on the photos they share and the way they communicate. Now, the company is planning to launch a new game that lets people compete against their real-life friends.

OK Cupid is one of the many companies that's tapping into the vast amount of data available about people based on their online behavior and connections. The company's research has shown that many women enjoy playing games with their friends, and that the most popular games are often the ones that appeal to men. To cater to these preferences, OK Cupid has created games that tap into these interests.

For instance, a new game for women focuses on collecting hearts for friends based on their daily activities, such as playing games, watching videos, or checking social media. Similarly, a game for girls aims to match women based on their interests, such as the books they read, the music they listen to, or their daily activity levels.

OK Cupid is also launching a new game called "Meet People" that makes it easier for users to connect with others based on shared interests. This mobile app is being tested in select cities, allowing users to swipe left or right to see if there's someone nearby with similar interests.

In the initial trial, two of OK Cupid's key customers in Austin, Texas, launched a small-scale app with local tech meetup attendees. The results were encouraging, with about 60% of users matching with someone at a tech meetup on a particular night.

For comparison, the same app had a 14% match rate when it first launched in August last year. OK Cupid plans to expand its gaming app to include more diverse groups and a broader range of interests, including both men and women from various demographics.

The company also plans to integrate its technology into other products, including its dating site, which connects millions of people worldwide.

One potential way to improve matchmaking effectiveness could be to enhance the technology itself. Currently, users must visit OK Cupid's site before swiping left or right, which can lead to issues on first dates. OK Cupid's technology might enable users to send more complex messages to friends.

However, one question remains unanswered: Does OK Cupid's technology actually work, or are there other limitations? A new study is investigating this.

A security feature called IsSystem helps determine whether a requested resource or system function output comes from a system process or a local process. For more information, see our article on Creating and Managing Resource Ownerships.

By default, IsSystem is set to SYSTEM, but there are exceptions.

For instance, if the requested resource is an existing process, a user process, or the result of a system function accessed through the CreateThread function, IsSystem sets the value to SYSTEM.

IsSystem doesn't always mean a resource isn't an output of a system process. There are other options to consider, which are outlined below. For a more comprehensive overview, see our Security Overview article.

If IsSystem indicates a process needs local privileges to access another process, it's set to the local system privilege. If it indicates a resource requires local privilege, it's set to the resource's local privilege.

In the realm of behavioral economics, the notion of bounded rationality posits that individuals' decision-making processes are influenced by the intricacies of their mental frameworks. This perspective suggests that people's choices are not always guided by a perfect rationality, but rather are shaped by a complex interplay of cognitive biases, emotional inclinations, and mental constraints.

Herbert Simon, an influential economist, first introduced the concept of bounded rationality in the mid-20th century. According to Simon, people's decision-making often deviates from the idealized notion of rationality espoused in traditional economic theory. Instead, decision-making is influenced by the limitations of human cognition and the availability of information.

The concept of bounded rationality has significant implications for understanding how people make decisions in real-world contexts. By acknowledging that decision-making is often imperfect and incomplete, bounded rationality provides valuable insights for fields such as management and public policy, where decision-makers frequently face uncertainty and incomplete information.

The initial paragraphs of Mark A. Niedermayer's article appear to be inconsequential. In my opinion, a credible report should be based on verifiable facts rather than personal opinions. The "evidence" presented in the article is marred by significant flaws, rendering it questionable.

This article relies heavily on the research conducted by Dr. Nita Forgacs, a psychologist at McGill University. However, it's crucial to note that Niedermayer was not involved in the study. At the time of publication, he was studying social cognition in dogs at the University of Florida.

The claim that children as young as six can process information about emotions, likes, and dislikes in others is astonishing. The study's authors propose that this finding supports the notion that children's cognitive abilities do not develop beyond adolescence. Dr. Forgacs remarks, "The fact that emotional abilities decline so dramatically so early in life is the biggest puzzle of child development research."

The issue lies in Niedermayer's inquiry. He's not questioning the validity or quality of this study or the study of emotions in animals. Instead, he's inquiring about how children are typically presented: in a positive light. I can't think of a reason why a study examining kids' reactions to their surroundings would be less relevant than the authors' approach.

Niedermayer claims that children as young as six can learn about human emotions. This assertion is unfounded, and I'll allow Niedermayer to address it.

The idea that six-year-olds can learn about other people and their emotions is counterintuitive. However, the notion that basic abilities can develop at a young age and that children's social competencies can be tested and proven at a young age has influenced the field of child development research. The idea of child development based on socialization rather than genetic development has also made significant advancements in our understanding of children's psychological, social, and biological origins.

One example of this approach is Dr. Forgacs' research showing that children's social knowledge at a young age and their ability to make inferences are crucial for learning about others. They can learn if another person thinks a certain way and it appears that these abilities depend on social situations. This new evidence confirms that there is a biological basis for developing social and cognitive skills. It's possible that as children begin to develop their basic social and cognitive skills, other areas of their development may rely on what they learn from others.

Niedermayer is creating a straw man argument, assuming that because he finds it unclear that children can learn to appreciate others' emotions, it would be foolish to assume that children lack social skills like understanding another person's point of view. He's incorrect, and not just because "a" is incorrect, but because we know better.

The story of human evolution is a captivating one, particularly when it comes to the human-chimp split. For most of their evolutionary history, human and ape ancestors were bipedal, but they developed legs later in most primate lineages. There's evidence that bipedalism evolved early in human evolution, and then some.

Two main types of researchers have contributed to our understanding of the human-chimp split. Dr. George Schaller, an anthropologist from Boston University, was a pioneer in both styles of research. Schaller was also known for his unconventional ideas. This week on The Sporkful, we're presenting a special three-part series exploring some of Schaller's most intriguing theories in human evolutionary history.

Schaller once proposed that the first bipedal hominins appeared around 1.2 million years ago, predating our own species. However, there are several issues with this theory: We're only just now discovering fossils that clearly demonstrate Homo erectus, the earliest known human species, walking upright. Other hominins of that age and later were bipedal, but there are no fossils that show them doing so.

Some animals don't develop legs after they develop, like hippos and anteaters. Instead, they develop arms later in life. In some cases, animals have legs and no arms in the same limb. Elephants are famous for this, typically having no arms at all, only legs. This makes their trunk an unusual shape.

Some researchers have also suggested that humans evolved from an ape ancestor that coexisted with other human species. This kind of human-animal hybridization might have occurred, and maybe even recently, but there are no clear signs of it.

When it comes to questions about human evolution, it's essential to consider anthropologists and palaeontologists as having different perspectives. While many palaeontologists study ancient animals, including fossils of plants and animals, anthropologists focus on living people, living human beings.

However, they don't always agree on the conclusions. Some anthropologists believe the human and chimp divergence was a one-time event, while others think there were changes in human anatomy that helped set humans and chimps apart. They all agree that there was significant overlap among the species that lived on this tiny island in Africa 20 million years ago. So, while it's crucial to remember that anthropologists discuss the same questions, they don't always agree on the answers. To facilitate a discussion between the two sides, we decided to invite them on a field trip.

This week, we've got some anthropologists from the Harvard Museum of Natural History in Cambridge joining us on The Sporkful podcast.

For more information on anthropological theory, visit the Museum of Anthropology's website.

For more discussion on Schaller's theories, listen to this episode with John Hawks and William Kimbel, both scholars of evolutionary biology. You can also check out the University of Washington's website, which has a collection of Schaller's papers, as well as the University of Wisconsin's collection. As we're using archival materials, we can't guarantee that it includes all of Schaller's papers.

In my previous column, I discussed the striking shift in U.S. crude oil exports. The country now imports fewer barrels of crude oil than it did just five years ago, which is both a blessing and a curse. On one hand, it means fewer goods to produce, but on the other hand, it also means fewer opportunities to import from abroad.

Between 2003 and 2014, U.S. oil exports were substantial, averaging almost 631,000 barrels per day and peaking at 674,000 barrels per day in July 2011. However, exports declined to just 1.5 million barrels per day in September 2014, the last year for which I have data. During this period, the U.S. enjoyed the third-largest export surplus worldwide, but it was also the longest-running surplus of any country.

Given this backdrop, one might expect exports to be thriving this year. Unfortunately, that's not the case. The percentage of petroleum and petroleum products in total imports has actually decreased since the last economic downturn.

Historically, recessions didn't typically lead to significant oil deficits. Today, however, there is a larger deficit than expected, and the export weakness doesn't appear to be linked to U.S. economic growth. In fact, exports have declined during each of the six quarters of the U.S. economic recovery.

It's challenging to pinpoint the factors contributing to this export performance, as there are numerous other factors at play during this recovery. The U.S. also imports significantly more from Canada than it exports to Canada, which has a significant impact on Canadian production levels. This is due in part to the fact that the U.S. uses a substantial amount of its own oil in Canada, and Canadian production has been increasing in recent years.

According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, the Canadian export-to-import balance for the third quarter of this year is roughly the same as it was a year ago. Canadian oil sands production reached approximately 2.6 million barrels per day in November, up from an annual decline of only 700,000 barrels in 2014. The EIA predicts that total Canadian exports will grow by 7 percent this year and exceed the 2.1 million-barrel annual rate in 2015.

I anticipate these numbers will continue to rise over the next few years as Canada's pipeline infrastructure matures and the economy picks up.

Richmond, Virginia, witnessed a diverse crowd gathering outside the federal court building, awaiting the appeals court's deliberation on Texas's stringent voter regulations. A black female pastor, along with gay couples, including two new parents, and members of a prominent immigrant group in Richmond, who were previously denied the right to vote in North Carolina, shared their concerns.

Michael H. Williams, a prominent civil rights attorney from the District, expressed his doubts about the Voting Rights Act's effectiveness, stating, "It seems like the Voting Rights Act is only for African Americans, and I don't think if the Supreme Court were to make a decision tomorrow, we would win this case."

Others argued that the case is more about enforcing state laws rather than voting rights. L.J. Davis, executive director of the Coalition to Defend the VRA, emphasized, "We're here in Richmond standing up for voting rights because voting rights in America have been under attack for too long."

When evaluating states' voting laws, factors such as compliance with the Voting Rights Act, the existence of a process to implement the law, and the potential for racial discrimination should be considered.

In Texas, the case primarily revolves around the voter ID law, which is considered one of the strictest in the country. The law requires proof of citizenship or a state-issued photo ID, with provisional ballots only being counted if a voter returns with a photo ID.

Supporters of the law argue that Texas is not required to demonstrate its efforts to ensure voting rights and should have the right to do so. Keith Ingram, a law professor at Texas A&M University, stated, "We are not required to do anything. The economic landscape has undergone a significant transformation since the 1970s. A striking aspect of this shift is the substantial increase in Americans who are neither employed nor actively seeking work. This phenomenon has led to a reevaluation of the traditional unemployment rate, which often overlooks the "marginally attached workers" who are eager to contribute to the labor market but struggle to find suitable opportunities.

The unemployment rate is a crucial indicator of labor market conditions, but it has its limitations. The recent rise in unemployment from 4.7% to 5% has resulted in a decline in the number of working Americans, primarily due to the difficulties faced by those seeking more hours. Moreover, the proportion of Americans classified as "marginally attached workers" has converged with the employment rate, suggesting that productivity gains are driving employment growth rather than an increase in the labor force participation rate.

Historically, labor force participation rates have exhibited a consistent pattern, with the number of individuals not in the labor force remaining relatively stable during recessions since 1979. However, the 2010 data reveals a distinct departure from this trend, as the labor force participation rate has plateaued despite the overall rate being slightly lower than in early 2008.

It is essential to recognize that labor force participation rates do not necessarily reflect the actual number of people working. By considering the percentage of individuals with jobs, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the labor market. For instance, if we assume a labor force participation rate of 66% and an employment rate of 56%, with 26% of those employed working part-time, the actual percentage of individuals with jobs would be 71%.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reports a labor force participation rate of 72%, indicating the percentage of individuals with jobs, including those who would like to work more hours if they could find suitable employment. This rate does not imply that individuals are not actively seeking work; rather, they are making conscious choices about their employment status.

The decline in labor force participation rates can be attributed to various factors, including the prolonged economic hardship experienced by individuals born between 1975 and 1999. The median net worth of households has decreased significantly, particularly among white households, which has led to a rise in the number of individuals seeking more hours or alternative employment opportunities.

What's more crucial to you than your professional integrity? For me, this question resonates deeply. As a journalist, I always prioritized the principle that anything published online should be something I'd be proud to share with my bosses. My own experience of being fired for writing too much, only to be punished for it, taught me that integrity is about personal honor and principle, not just what's expedient.

A similar question, "What's more important to you than your professional reputation?" comes from the White House, the same administration that once fired journalists for reporting "fake news" and created a system to punish those who reported it. This time, the question targets the administration itself, which used an executive order to punish four major news organizations for reporting "fake news."

The key difference lies in punishing media corporations for their journalists' actions versus targeting members of Congress who pass laws that allegedly violate the executive order. One wonders if there's any real difference between the two. In both cases, the government creates its own rules and punishes independent media for doing their job. The government is punishing an institution that's supposed to serve the people, not just its members or those with a certain partisan view.

The fact that Trump claims it's not "real news" that the administration fears is telling. The president is so afraid of actual people asking questions that he's creating obstacles and blaming journalists for it. But here's the thing: the president doesn't care if his enemies believe him or not. If the White House truly believes some media is doing too much of the public's work, they have the right to tell the government to do its job while punishing the media for doing it. Trump has convinced the country that his presidency isn't difficult to manage, only that some people make it harder.

This doesn't mean the United States will have any journalism left after this move. There will be a process of erosion where journalists will lose their independence and be forced to work for a government that values only its own power. Journalists deserve more than punishment for their work, but Trump has effectively done that for them.

I recall the initial amusement I felt upon encountering this phrase. Upon its second appearance, I discovered it referred to a notion that piqued my interest.

For those unfamiliar, I'll clarify that I'm not opposed to the concept of conspiracy theories, as long as they're grounded in reality. In fact, I've found myself in the minority among skeptics, having lived in a country where the news is generally trustworthy.

Until recently, I've approached conspiracy theories with a healthy dose of skepticism, often dismissing them as unfounded. However, I've come to realize that there's more to the story.

I'd like to share my observations on the various types of conspiracy theories I've encountered. If you're not prepared for my explanation, you may want to explore other sources.

There are five primary types of conspiracy theories that have caught my attention:

1. Government Involvement

It's possible that this notion won't surprise you, and I might attribute the blame to the media, which often sensationalizes news and creates misconceptions. After all, most people do make assumptions based on incomplete information.

2. Government Alteration of Historical Events

This theory posits that powerful organizations, like the Bilderberg Group, secretly shape global events. The recent WikiLeaks leaks provide a compelling example.

Personally, I view the CIA's reluctance to disclose information about life in the Soviet Union under Stalin as a prime example of secrecy.

3. Government Encouragement of Paranoia

This theme ran throughout many conspiracy theories I've encountered. The government allegedly aims to control every aspect of our lives by spreading misinformation.

4. Government Malice

The 9/11 conspiracy theory is a prime example of this phenomenon. The lack of concrete information and the emphasis on government involvement only fueled speculation.

5. Government Superiority

As someone who values critical thinking, I find most conspiracy theories unconvincing. I believe that cognitive dissonance plays a significant role in the proliferation of these theories.

Ultimately, I'm drawn to the idea that the government is indeed intelligent and capable, but the notion of their omnipotence is unlikely.

A former CEO of a prominent PR agency now serving in Congress expressed concern that companies might shy away from seeking government assistance due to the potential for lucrative contracts to be compromised.

"There are various factors that can trigger the contracting process to shut down," said Paul Stott, who led the government's Public Relations and Public Affairs Department from 2000 to 2015. "People are hesitant to seek government help because they fear it might be perceived as a liability, so they opt out."

The issue is particularly pressing given an ongoing review of government support for the private sector by the Government Accountability Office. The review concluded that government-industry ties have exceeded historical levels, yet the federal government is still grappling with how to ensure its support does not hinder private sector job growth.

The GAO emphasized the importance of ensuring that government support does not conflict with the government's core responsibilities to serve the nation's best interests. Congress has driven federal support to the private sector, with lawmakers seeking to provide funding and services in areas like homeland security, research, and public-private partnerships.

However, with more government employees facing budget cuts and the federal workforce growing as a share of the overall population, the issue of how the government will maintain its support, especially in regards to jobs, is a sensitive topic for many lawmakers.

The GAO report noted that some outside help is available to smaller agencies seeking to improve their performance, but federal support may be too large for many agencies to provide.

Congress has made some key changes since the GAO report was completed in 2015. Government grants and contracts have increased, and the Office of Management and Budget has launched an initiative to find ways for the federal government to become more competitive by attracting private money.

The idea is that agencies that can hire more people and offer higher pay will attract and retain more private sector business. This concept is not new but has gained momentum in recent years following high-profile scandals and the government's need to balance its budget.

Some companies have already implemented measures to protect themselves against government demands. For instance, IBM requires its employees with government contracts to disclose the type of private sector work they performed and the price of the services.

As the government and public become more aware of how many jobs flow to the private sector from the government, companies may become more cautious about seeking assistance, experts said.

The GAO reviewed federal agencies' support for private sector job growth during fiscal 2015, during which the federal workforce grew by 13.3% to about 188.5 million workers. The report found that federal jobs increased by 16 million, with the majority coming from the private sector.

However, the GAO did not have access to sufficient information to estimate how many jobs could eventually come from the public sector because some jobs might be created through a combination of internal hires and outside help.

"We don't know how many jobs the government can create," said William Sullivan, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution who served as GAO's executive secretary at the time of the report. "Are they growing at 20% or 12%? How are they doing with the population increase? That's what we need to know to help the federal government get the right incentives for itself to be able to do more of these kinds of jobs."

Despite this setback, Enbridge remains committed to the project, having already built a pipeline to Canada.

According to a draft agreement, the pipeline would stretch 11,000 kilometers, from northern Puebla, Mexico, to the Gulf Coast, where it would terminate in Texas. The pipeline would transport approximately 900,000 barrels of crude oil per day, equivalent to roughly 4% of Mexico's current oil production.

Enbridge has indicated that it would need to acquire necessary land and reroute the pipeline to comply with US safety regulations. However, the Mexican government has yet to weigh in on the project.

If approved, it could have a profound impact on the country's energy exports and economic stability. However, the decision ultimately hinges on negotiations over a new trade deal between the US and Mexico, which is expected to be finalized by the end of the year.

A draft proposal from the Mexican government outlines several requirements for the project, including the need for Enbridge to demonstrate its ability to complete the project with minimal disruption. The agreement also stipulates that the pipeline must be constructed using a technique that complies with national, state, and international building codes.

In addition to security requirements, the project would also need to undergo a strict construction process, including an independent review of each element of the project. The review would assess the integrity of the pipeline, its design and capacity, and the safety of the required pipeline structures.

For Mexico and the US, the key issue is the length of the project. Mexican diplomats argue that this project is too crucial to Mexico's economy to ignore. The project would provide access to major oil and gas discoveries, improve Mexico's energy security, and open up a vital new route for global commerce.

However, Pena Nieto's government is not in favor of the project, stating that there is no agreement with Enbridge. The Mexican administration is only interested in promoting a new trade deal between the US and Mexico.

What's the Difference Between the Two Math Programs?

We have two math departments at UT Austin: the Department of Mathematics and the Department of Statistics. Both programs offer undergraduate and graduate degrees, with a focus on statistics and probability. The graduate program in statistics includes a specialization in Bayesian statistics.

For example, the Bachelor of Fine Arts (BFA) in Statistics offers students a focus on statistics, while the math major offers a concentration in probability and statistics. (For more information on the differences between the majors, please see the page on Degrees at UT Austin)

Why Can't I Take Math 1-11?

Mathematics 1-11 is a rigorous undergraduate program with three or four courses that provide a broad and deep foundation in mathematical techniques. Mathematics 11-12 is a rigorous upper-division program with two or three courses that provide a broad and deep foundation in advanced and applied mathematical techniques. Computers with 128-bit processing power are theoretically feasible, but their practical applications are limited. Several factors contribute to this: firstly, the cost of developing such systems would be substantial, necessitating the use of cutting-edge and costly hardware. This would, in turn, make the technology inaccessible to the general public. Secondly, most software is optimized for 64-bit architecture, rendering significant rewrites necessary to accommodate 128-bit systems. This would be a time-consuming and resource-intensive endeavor. Furthermore, the performance benefits of 128-bit computers over their 64-bit counterparts would be minimal, failing to justify the added expense and compatibility issues. Ultimately, the advantages of 128-bit computers are outweighed by the practical challenges and costs. As a result, we continue to utilize 64-bit systems, which effectively cater to the needs of most users at a more reasonable price point.

If you're a gamer, you might be interested in finding Xbox games after finishing a game. You can easily search for games on the Xbox Games Store, but searching for games on Xbox SmartGlass is a bit more complicated.

To start, navigate to the Xbox Hub on your SmartGlass, where you'll find all your game data and favorite games. From there, click the Search All section in the top right corner and select the filter options you prefer. I chose Xbox One games, Xbox 360 games, and all Xbox games to get the most comprehensive results.

However, I found that none of the games are labeled, making it difficult to filter the results. Most of the Xbox 360 games listed are actually for Xbox 360, not Xbox 360 SmartGlass. This can be frustrating, especially when you're trying to find specific games.

One workaround is to use Windows Explorer. Right-click on a file or folder on your PC and select Save Target As. Make sure the Target Location is set to the same location in OneDrive for Windows 10. Then, right-click the Save Target As link and browse to the location where you saved the file. From there, select your save location and you're good to go.

Alternatively, you can disable the Microsoft SmartGlass app on your Xbox 360 and restart your console. This will allow you to use the Xbox 360 Xbox SmartGlass app on your Windows 10 device.

To do this, open Windows Settings, search for SmartGlass, and disable it. This will also disable any additional SmartGlass features for your controller. Then, head to OneDrive for Windows 10 and search for 'Xbox 360 Xbox App for Windows 10'. You'll find the app in the 'Your apps' section, and you can use it to search for Xbox 360 games.

Overall, searching for Xbox 360 games on Xbox SmartGlass can be a bit of a challenge, but with the right workaround, you can find the games you're looking for.

The Eucharistic Table from the S. Trena Papyrus in Egypt presents a captivating image. The initial line refers to the "bread of immortality," capable of sustaining even the deceased. The subsequent lines discuss the "bread of life," distributed to the faithful in churches during the early Christian era.

The third line describes two types of bread, one for the body and one for the spirit. Noticeably, the bread for the body does not contain gluten. The final line specifies that the preparation of this bread is entrusted to the "priest and deacons."

The Eucharist is composed of various elements, which can be categorized into three parts. The first part consists of the "bread of the living" accompanied by "signet wine." The second part is the bread for the body, and the third part is the holy chalice, where the body and blood of Christ are "set forth."

The Eucharist encompasses numerous "signs and tokens" that are given to individuals, either voluntarily or involuntarily. It is also referred to as the "cup of blessing," as the associated signs and tokens are blessed and utilized by the Eucharistic community during the celebration of sacraments.

It is essential to note that, according to the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the body of Christ is not treated as a mere vessel to be blessed by the priest or "blessed" by the minister. Christ, as the "head of the Church," is the supreme priestly sacrament, and His institution of the Eucharist is necessary.

The Blessed Sacrament

During the administration of the sacrament, the priest first receives or prepares the "bread" through a blessing from the bishop. The bread is then placed on a linen cloth, wrapped in new linen cloth, and sealed with the chalice dipped in the Holy Spirit.

When the priest combines the sacred vessels, the wine, referred to as the "holy chalice," is poured into the cup by the celebrant. The wine is poured in a procession with the bread and chalice. The chalice is not filled at once; rather, it is filled by one, then two, then three, and so on, up to the number of the faithful.

The priests then wash the chalice with white wine and pour holy water upon it, dipping the chalice in it. The water enters the chalice at the end, where it meets the oil from the olive tree. The chalice is then brought to the place of prayer of the faithful, where the faithful and the priest stand together for a prayer.

The People

The priest, attired in his vestments, consecrates the bread and chalice to the people, just as they have been consecrated to him by the bishop. However, the priest presents the bread and chalice to the people with reverence, as he does when he consecrates them. Thus, the priest brings the bread and wine to the church in obedience to the bishop, and the people, with reverence, bring them to the altar in obedience to the priest.

The Celebrant

In the celebration of the Eucharist, there are two celebrants. During the beginning of the service, after the priest has blessed the bread and chalice with the bishop, there is a singing of the liturgies, sometimes one and sometimes the other.

Gather a bowl, and combine eggs with a cup of water. Blend the mixture with a gentle touch for approximately one minute. Remove the whisk from the bowl. Add a pinch of vinegar, roughly half a teaspoon, and stir for an additional minute. Once the mixture has reached the desired consistency, remove the whisk. Transfer the bowl to a larger container. When we try to capture a signal, like a sound or image, it can get lost in translation if our sampling rate isn't quite right. This is called aliasing, and it's like trying to paint a masterpiece with a brush that's too small. The details get fuzzy, and the end result is a mess.

Let's say you're trying to record a sweet melody with your phone, but the mic just can't handle the complexity of the sound. The recording comes out all muddled and unrecognizable. That's aliasing in action.

Now, the Nyquist frequency is like a secret ingredient that makes all the difference. It's the highest frequency that our sampling rate can accurately capture. If we're trying to record something with a higher frequency, it's like trying to translate a foreign language – it just won't work. The Nyquist frequency is like the border that separates the frequencies we can handle from the ones we can't. If a sound tries to sneak across that border, it'll get distorted, like a person trying to sneak into a country without the right papers.

"We're in a predicament with our public education system," stated Daniel Losen, executive director of the National Center for Education Statistics. "It's a pressing issue that requires immediate attention. The short-term effects are alarming, and we must address them regularly."

This is particularly true as public schools struggle to adapt to an increasing number of students with disabilities and states attempt to reduce educational spending. The federal government is expected to provide a steady flow of funds for educational services, but we're not seeing the same level of support as we did eight years ago.

Some states, like Rhode Island, have taken on significant debt to balance their budgets. Michigan, for instance, cut nearly $8 billion from its budget last year to balance its books. Other states, such as Alabama and Indiana, have implemented significant tax cuts to fund education, often closing tax loopholes. However, some states are shifting more responsibility to parents, who are paying higher prices and receiving reduced public services.

The idea behind these approaches is that increased spending has a stronger impact on students' success. However, some experts argue that it can be challenging for school systems, especially those with budget shortfalls, to make the necessary changes.

"If we're going to have a meaningful conversation about what's best for students, we need to consider who is responsible for education funding," said Charles R. Jones, a professor of public policy and public affairs at Penn State University. "The current system doesn't work for a large share of students, and the debate is not just about numbers, but also about how we design and implement our public education system."

Some states have adopted a model called "parent trigger laws," which allows parents to take control of their children's education, often at a significant cost. At least a dozen states have tried to pass laws like those in Kansas and Alabama, which provide more public funding to public schools based on student performance.

A few states have taken an extreme approach, increasing per-pupil expenditures despite deep budget shortfalls. Arizona, for example, had one of the highest per-student expenditures in the nation before implementing a plan to increase spending by 5.4 percent. However, the state legislature rejected a bill that would have increased public school spending by 2 percent and another that would have increased per-student spending by 5 percent.

In the end, the state passed a plan that would have raised spending by 1 percent a year over nine years, at a cost of $2.2 billion. Similar increases have been approved in Louisiana, Maine, and other states facing budget shortfalls.

"Parent trigger plans are not effective solutions, despite understandable and legitimate arguments," said Michael J. Petrilli, a lawyer for the Thomas B. Fordham Institute, a conservative think tank.

States argue that such programs put them in an impossible position, as it's difficult to predict the impact of additional funding. Some opponents claim that these programs divert funds from other essential services.

Airborne condensation trails, a byproduct of flight, manifest as wispy clouds trailing behind aircraft. These ephemeral formations arise from the condensation of atmospheric water vapor, which occasionally freezes into delicate ice crystals. This phenomenon, entirely natural and benign, poses no threat to human health or the environment.



In stark contrast, a widespread misconception has taken hold, proposing that airplanes deliberately disperse chemicals into the atmosphere as part of a clandestine government initiative. Regrettably, empirical evidence and credible authorities in meteorology and aviation have consistently debunked this unfounded notion.



In summary, contrails are an inherent aspect of air travel, governed by the laws of physics and thermodynamics. Chemtrails, on the other hand, remain a baseless, unfounded conspiracy theory, lacking empirical support and credibility.

The evolution of American public-school education has been a gradual process, with each step building upon the last. However, it's essential to acknowledge that the path forward is not without its challenges. The concept of education and democracy must be reevaluated to accommodate the complexities of the 21st century. This requires a shift in our collective understanding and a willingness to adapt to new ideas and perspectives.

In the early 2000s, there was a growing recognition of the education system's potential to shape individual choices and life outcomes. The Bush administration's "No Child Left Behind" initiative was a well-intentioned effort to address educational disparities. However, it ultimately perpetuated a neoliberal market model, which has had far-reaching consequences.

The rise of the Tea Party, anti-union sentiment, and the "teach-to-the-test" movement have significantly altered the educational landscape. It's astonishing to consider how quickly attitudes have shifted, from a focus on student-centered learning to an emphasis on standardized testing and accountability measures.

I recall a conversation with a colleague in 2007, who expressed concerns about the impact of "teach-to-the-test" on student learning. They believed that this approach would ultimately undermine the value of education. Unfortunately, this sentiment has been largely overshadowed by the prevailing narrative.

As I began my tenure as an education faculty member in 2008, I was struck by the disconnect between the rhetoric and reality of education policy. A colleague, Eileen O'Neill, was a vocal supporter of education reform, despite being a member of a teachers' union. Her perspective highlights the complexities and contradictions within the education system.

The story of Eileen O'Neill serves as a reminder that our understanding of education is often influenced by our personal experiences and biases. It's essential to acknowledge the limitations of our knowledge and be open to alternative perspectives.

The challenges facing the education system are multifaceted and deeply ingrained. Teachers' salaries, for instance, are often shrouded in mystery, with varying levels of transparency and accountability. It's crucial that we address these issues head-on, rather than relying on superficial solutions.

Ultimately, the future of American public-school education hangs in the balance. By acknowledging the complexities and challenges, we can work towards a more equitable and effective system that prioritizes the needs of students and teachers alike.

AUSTIN, Texas - A federal judge has put on hold a plan to withhold millions of dollars from Planned Parenthood, a move that was met with opposition from the organization. The plan was part of a lawsuit filed by an anti-abortion group last year.

Planned Parenthood clinics in Texas, Louisiana, and Alabama were already under a temporary restraining order, preventing them from receiving any funds in the case. The judge's decision was written in part by Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who had sued over a law that banned abortions in Texas and blocked funding for the clinics.

The judge's ruling stated that Planned Parenthood was already receiving the required amount of funding, and that withholding more would cause harm. The Obama administration had sought to punish Planned Parenthood over a video released by a conservative anti-abortion group, which showed clinics offering fetal tissue from abortions.

Planned Parenthood thanked Governor Abbott and the state of Texas for their efforts to defund the organization, and said they would continue to fight for women's health and dignity. A Planned Parenthood spokeswoman said the decision was a win for women's health, as it means taxpayers will not be forced to fund the organization.

Last year, Texas legislators cut funding to Planned Parenthood, and Governor Abbott has said he wants to cut funding outright. Planned Parenthood has accused the Obama administration of a "political vendetta" and is also fighting a separate lawsuit over the president's move to block subsidies for abortion coverage.

The University of Michigan is thrilled to announce the launch of its U-M Emergency Medicine Residency program in a brand-new location in Detroit. This initiative was made possible thanks to a generous $1.4 million donation from the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation.

"We recognize the pressing need for skilled emergency medicine professionals, and we're committed to providing our residents with the most cutting-edge training possible," said Dr. Mark Schlissel, U-M Medical Chair, U-M Professor, and University of Michigan President. "With this funding, we're excited to welcome students who will benefit from our state-of-the-art facilities and expert faculty."

The U-M Emergency Medicine Residency program will be based in Detroit, where it will be the only program in Michigan authorized to provide emergency care without the use of PICC lines. Instead, the facility will feature a new on-site cardiac catheterization lab. Residents will train in three interventional-critical care units, including UPMC Mercy and Wayne County hospitals, as well as a fully equipped intensive care unit.

"We're honored to welcome the U-M Emergency Medicine Residency team to our practice," said Mike St. George, U-M Hospital Chief. "Their reputation for excellence in emergency medicine is unmatched, and we're confident that every patient who enters our facilities will receive the highest level of care."

The U-M Emergency Medicine Residency program was established in 2010, with an initial class of 30 residents. Since then, the program has grown and evolved, training some of the world's largest emergency and trauma teams.
